#4928. 35 Best Home Gym Equipment Items to Build Your Gym, Tested By Us

This gear will make you never want to leave your personal fitness sanctuary.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHETHER YOU'RE A weightlifter, CrossFit acolyte, cardio junkie, or yoga lover, a dependable home gym setup is a must. You might not have the square footage or budget to create a space that replicates your go-to health club or weight room space, but you can still achieve great workouts at home with the best home gym equipment.

Building your home fitness setup should prioritize space, functionality, and usability over trends. Choose gear that suits your needs and storage space. Whether it's a full-on garage gym or portable equipment, the best home gym equipment can help you make the most of your home workouts.

Read more: How Men's Health Thoroughly Tests and Reviews Fitness Products

From traditional heavy lifting (we love these barbell sets and weight benches) to HIIT workouts (this 15-minute interval workout is sure to make you sweat) to full-on indoor cardio rigs (like the best indoor rowing machines and the best ellipticals), we've tested and vetted something out there for every type of training imaginable. In fact, we've used hundreds of pieces of equipment throughout the years, from the most high-end, commercial-grade options all the way down to budget gear from Amazon. Our extensive testing process has involved a comprehensive evaluation of multiple factors, including durability, performance, suitability for different fitness levels, and value, to ensure that we recommend only the best.

SMRTFT’s Nüobell is the perfect ultra-durable adjustable dumbbell for my home workouts. It can easily be five pounds, perfect for warm-up work, or 80 pounds, enough to challenge most people on fundamental leg moves, Eric Sung, C.S.C.S., a member of the Men's Health Strength in Diversity initiative and trainer at Performance Lab in New York City, told us.

These adjustable dumbbells give you the convenience of 16 sets of dumbbells all in one compact footprint. They're easy to use and offer superior durability thanks to their machined steel weight plates. If you're starting a home gym from scratch or live in tight confines with little room to spare, consider these a must-have. Few items pack as much versatility and return on investment in such a small package.

PowerBlock is practically synonymous with adjustable dumbbells—and for good reason. The Pro 100 model is compact, rugged, and replaces an entire weight rack. With a range from 5 to 100 pounds, it offers more versatility than almost any other dumbbell on the market.

One of our testers, Maillard Howell, who tried PowerBlock’s Pro 50 model, said he liked how compact the dumbbells were and that the square shape lets you set them down without rolling away. Men’s Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., likes how easy they are to adjust. He’s also dropped these dumbbells from about four feet and reported zero breakage (though we wouldn’t suggest dropping them).

There’s not much to nitpick with these dumbbells. That said, they can feel awkward and obtrusive during specific exercises. For example, because your hand and wrist are inside the bell, they can feel clunky during dumbbell curls. Samuel says the weight distribution differs between PowerBlocks and traditional dumbbells, and he sticks with the latter for most accessory movements (biceps curls, skull crushers, lateral raises, etc.).

We dubbed this bench the “mid-range bench that delivers big value”. For around $350, we’re confident the AB-3000 is nicer than any bench you’ve used in a commercial gym and can serve most lifters for years. It offers flat, incline, and decline options, which most adjustable benches on the market don’t. You’ll never outlift the 1,000-pound weight capacity, and the redesigned 2.0 version features a longer back leg to eliminate side-to-side wobble.

“Hands down, my favorite feature is the ladder-style adjustment system—you can drag the bench to any upright angle in seconds,” says NASM-certified personal trainer and product tester Andrew Gutman.

There are a few trade-offs. The 2.1-inch pad gap, while common among adjustable benches, could bother some lifters if their hips land in the gap mid-set. The bench also can’t be stored upright, and at nearly five feet long, it claims a chunk of floor space. Lastly, while $350 is a fair price for this level of quality, it’s not exactly pocket change.

Read More: Our Review of the Rep Fitness AB-3000

Hammer Strength (by Life Fitness) outfits weight rooms for elite organizations—from the Tennessee Titans to Team USA Bobsled. And for good reason: When it comes to quality, dependability, and customization, Hammer Strength sets the gold standard. Even the Men’s Health weight room features Hammer Strength’s Elite iD Half Rack.

The HD NX rack is highly customizable. You can choose between two heights (86" or 91"), two storage depths (15" or 21"), and either four or six uprights. It's essentially a commercial-grade system adapted for home use. That is if your “home gym” resembles a college weight room. Before buying, measure your space carefully and consider your long-term training plans. Even in its slimmest configuration, the HD NX commands serious square footage.

But with that footprint comes unmatched functionality. You can outfit it with almost anything: multiple pull-up bar variations, band pegs, barbell storage, Nordic curl attachments, and more. The rack works with a wide range of accessories and is built to withstand hard workouts year after year.

The HD NX is the best rack money can buy, but you’ll need a lot of it. It’s overkill for most lifters, but for those building the ultimate home gym with no budget restrictions, this is the crown jewel. It’s a lifetime investment you’ll never regret.

Foldable squat racks are a game-changer for home gyms, and Titan’s T-3 Series rack offers one of the best values. When not in use, it folds flat to just five inches off the wall. Unfolded, it gives you the option of 21” or 41” of depth, with a substantial 1,100-pound weight capacity, more than enough for even serious lifters. It also comes with J-hooks (essential for racking your barbell) and a pull-up bar for added versatility.

This space-saver does come with trade-offs. Like most folding racks, it requires wall mounting, and the necessary hardware isn’t included. You’ll also want to make sure your wall can support both the 145-pound rack and the load you plan to lift. Even when mounted properly, a wall-mounted rack may feel less stable than a fully bolted-down or freestanding unit.

That said, for under $400 shipped (and with a one-year warranty), the T-3 delivers beyond its price point. It’s a no-frills, budget-friendly rack that doesn’t skimp on strength or functionality, ideal for anyone building a legit home gym in limited space.

This seven-foot Olympic barbell has been one of our favorite home barbells for years. The 15" sleeves are designed with snap clips to accommodate any 2-inch Olympic plates. It's built of 110,000 PSI tensile strength cold-rolled Japanese steel with a black oxide finish, so it's plenty durable. It's durable enough, in fact, to be rated to 1,000 pounds. That won't quite accommodate powerlifters, but it's more than enough for beginner to intermediate home lifters.

Most reviewers say it feels great in the hands (even without the knurled grip), though some report more bending than expected when lifting 350 pounds or more. But at roughly half the price of most premium alternatives, it's an incredible value, especially for any moderate weightlifters looking to upgrade their home gym without spending a small fortune.

REP Fitness' rubber bumper plates strike a strong balance of affordability and durability. Built with stainless steel inserts for easy loading and a stylish black high-density rubber, these plates are designed to take a beating, whether you’re deadlifting in the garage or doing Olympic lifts on a platform.

For those looking for a complete set, with color coding for different weights, REP Fitness also offers one with five different plates—10 lb (grey), 15 lb (black), 25 lb (green), 35 lb (yellow), and 45 lb (blue)—and for the cost of $775, you can get everything you need to get started. We recommend starting with four to six plates to get your home gym rolling, then adding more as needed.

For lifters who want solid performance without premium pricing, these REP Fitness plates offer great value on the market.

CAP Barbell's cast iron plates strike the right balance between affordability and durability. Built with a precision-machined 2-inch center hole for a secure fit on Olympic barbells. The plates feature a durable black baked enamel finish and are built to take a beating, whether you’re deadlifting in the garage or doing Olympic lifts on a platform.

For those looking for a complete set, with color coding for different weights, Titan also offers four additional plates—10 lb (grey), 25 lb (green), 35 lb (yellow), and 45 lb (blue)—and for the cost of $518, you can get everything you need to get started. We recommend starting with four to six plates to get your home gym rolling, then adding more as needed.

For lifters who want solid performance without premium pricing, these Titan Fitness plates offer great value on the market.

Adjustable dumbbells save space, but nothing beats the feel of individual iron in your hands. Fixed dumbbells are sturdier, more durable, and have fully knurled chrome handles for a secure, grippy feel—especially when sweating through a tough set. They’re also better suited for circuit-style training, since you don’t need to adjust weights between exercises.

REP Fitness’s Hex Dumbbell Set delivers commercial-gym quality for your home. You can choose from three weight ranges (5-50 lbs, 5-75 lbs, or 5-100 lbs) and pair them with a sleek rack in black, red, or blue. We especially love the chrome handles: They’re knurled end to end for a grippy, no-slip feel that feels premium.

That said, a complete dumbbell set takes up space. Lots of space. The 100-pound set weighs more than 2,000 pounds and spans about six feet of horizontal real estate. It's also not cheap. But if you want the real gym experience at home, these dumbbells are built to outlast your training career.

This adjustable kettlebell from Titan Fitness is “best for beginners” because it nails the fundamentals: It’s reasonably priced (around $150), adjusts from 10 to 40 pounds in seconds, and takes up the same amount of space as a pair of shoes. The weight range covers most beginner-friendly kettlebell movements—from presses and rows to goblet squats, curls, and even cleans and snatches.

If you’re a casual lifter looking to mix in the occasional kettlebell finisher, this one will serve you well. That said, more experienced users will quickly bump against the 40-pound ceiling, especially for swings and deadlifts. And while the plastic housing is sturdy, it doesn’t match the longevity or feel of solid cast iron.

Still, for anyone just getting into kettlebell training, this is the best entry-level option on the market—and a smart way to add variety without cluttering your gym.

Read More: The 6 Best Adjustable Kettlebells

Austin-based Kettlebell Kings has become a small powerhouse in the world of home gym equipment—and these powder-coated models are no exception. Made from single-cast iron with a smooth-yet-grippy powder coat finish, these kettlebells are built to withstand endless swings, snatches, and cleans. The 18 available weight options (ranging from 9 to 106 pounds) make it easy to scale up over time, and the color-coded bands around the handles let you identify weights at a glance.

That quality comes at a cost. Kettlebell Kings’ kettlebells sit at the higher end of the price range—expect to pay around $500 for a full set. But if you want top-tier, American-made bells that’ll last forever, start here. "Whether I’m repping through a set of swings or snatches, I know I can depend on the durable, powder-coated weights," says MH Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM.

Metal kettlebells are pricey. And they’re not exactly gentle on your wrists or floors. GoRuck’s Sand Kettlebell is a soft-sided alternative built for tough workouts and easy transport. Shaped like a traditional kettlebell, this canvas training tool can be filled with sand (not included), emptied when not in use, and folded up for on-the-go sessions.

It’s rugged as hell. The double-seal filling system keeps sand from leaking mid-workout. The padded handles add comfort, and GoRuck uses double-pass stitching and a reinforced base to keep the bag from falling apart, even after years of swings, presses, throws, and drops.

Just know this isn’t a direct substitute for a cast-iron bell. If you’re training for kettlebell sport or focusing on technique-heavy movements like snatches or Turkish get-ups, this won’t replicate the same feel. But for general strength and conditioning, it’s a versatile, joint-friendly, and durable option at a fraction of the price.

Plyo box workouts are a great way to build explosive strength, but not at the expense of your shins. REP’s soft plyo boxes feature a wood core and a high-density foam exterior wrapped in grippy vinyl, offering a good balance of structure and comfort.

They come in three heights—16, 20, and 24 inches—and arrive fully assembled. The soft covering helps muffle noise and reduces injury risk if you miss a rep. And while they’re relatively lightweight, each box can handle up to 400 pounds, making them suitable for bigger athletes or weighted jump work.

One thing to note: These boxes aren’t ideal on slick surfaces like tile, polished wood, or smooth concrete. They need some grip to stay put during explosive movements (we’ve made this mistake before). Also, the narrow footprint may feel less stable during lateral movements or box step-overs.

Still, for most home gym users, the REP Plyo Boxes offer a safer, quieter, and more versatile upgrade over the typical wooden box.

Read More: The 7 Best Plyo Boxes According to Certified Trainers

The Hydrow Wave earned a spot on our 2025 Men's Health Home Gym Awards. It pairs a sleek, compact design with surprisingly tranquil, waterway-inspired workouts. Unlike traditional rowers that use noisy air resistance (looking at you, Concept2), the Hydrow Wave uses magnetic resistance for a whisper-quiet ride that won’t disturb the rest of the house.

Yes, it’s pricey. And yes, you’ll need a monthly subscription. But Hydrow’s instructor-led, on-the-water sessions are so vivid and immersive that even longer workouts fly by. Samuel said it feels like you’re actually on the water, and his workouts rarely felt boring on this rower. When your workout is over, just fold it up and store it vertically to save space.

Our only gripe? You can’t skip the scenic classes and program your own intervals. Still, for most users, the guided experience is the main appeal. And when you’re done, the Wave folds upright for easy storage.

The Concept2 RowErg is the standard by which all rowing machines are measured, a device that can redline your heart rate in minutes and is perfect for strengthening hips, glutes, back, and core.

The RowErg with Standard Legs is the new name for Concept2's RowErg rower, and it's the first device that comes to mind when we think of training on a rower at home. Our editors have never been on a better rower than this one, point blank. In a nutshell, it offers many of the same features as the best rowing machines that cost twice as much.

"It's an industry standard used by CrossFit and in many high-profile competitions for a reason," Samuel says. "It relies on a variable resistance flywheel that provides a constant challenge, making it great for high volume or experienced rowers."

It's also extremely easy to assemble (you can see a video of us assembling it here). In our experience (and many Amazon reviewers agree), setup takes around 20 minutes with minimal tools or hardware (just eight screws are required). City dwellers and space-conscious users will appreciate the clever design that lets this machine separate into two pieces for easy storage. Built-in caster wheels make setup and put-away a breeze. Plus, it's surprisingly affordable. This is the definitive home rowing experience.

You can spend $25, $70, even $150 on a jump rope. But you don’t have to. After testing dozens, Men’s Health editors agree: The $6 BOOMIBOO Skipping Rope offers the best bang for your buck. It’s lightweight, durable, and surprisingly smooth thanks to ball-bearing rotation in the handles.

I’ve used this rope regularly for over a year, and it’s held up better than expected. The bearings spin clean, and the foam handles are easy on the hands. My only issue with it is that the length feels a bit off out of the package. You can adjust it (it comes at 9 feet), but I never bothered. I just widened my arms, and it still did the job.

Unless you’re chasing double-unders or elite-level speed, this rope is more than enough—and the price is tough to beat.

Read More: Best Jumping Ropes, Tested By Us

This adjustable weighted jump rope is made of thick silicone that is soft, sweat-resistant, and comfortable for long workouts. Our testing confirms this jump rope is built to last. Out of the box, it's nearly 10 feet long, but is designed to be cut to achieve the perfect fit based on user height. This is ideal for a single user, but doesn't lend itself well to multiple users within the same household unless they're the same height.

Together, the rope and handles weigh 1 pound, so this kit is enough to challenge you during a good cardio sesh. At around $20, this is another great budget-friendly option for anyone looking to get in some cardio at home without a huge piece of equipment.

When you're looking for an exercise bike that's as high-tech as it gets, the Peloton Bike is still our go-to choice. The 22-inch HD touchscreen display is crisp and easy to use, and its library of best-in-class instructor-led studio-style classes is a true game-changer for home workouts. Our editors have used this bike for more than four years now, and have never run out of fresh classes to try.

For nearly $1500, it's a bummer that users need to shell out an additional $24/month for full access to the platform. But for the many Peloton users who have found community in their classes and on the leaderboard, the cost is more than worth it.

Read More: The Best Exercise Bikes, Tested by Us

Manual treadmills may look intimidating, but they have surged in popularity for good reason: They make you work harder, respond instantly to your pace, and run quieter than motorized options. The REP Fitness Strive Treadmill is a standout in the category; it’s a durable curved treadmill that honors its promise as a manuel treadmill and adds a sled push to the equation.

At over 418 pounds, we suggest building this treadmill where you want it and avoid moving it up and down stairs. Still, built-in front wheels let you reposition it if needed. The 400-pound weight capacity makes it a solid pick for larger users, and REP Fitness backs its promise with a 5-year frame warranty—essentially guaranteeing long-term durability.

Yes, it’s big. Yes, it costs almost $4,000. But for runners or serious home gym owners looking for a low-maintenance, high-performance machine, the Strive Treadmill is a wise investment.

NordicTrack is a giant in the treadmill game, and the T10 hits the sweet spot for home gym owners. It’s more compact than the brand’s Commercial 1750, yet still boasts a full-size 60-inch running belt—long enough for sprinting and tall runners alike. Plus, it folds up for easier storage between workouts.

Despite its smaller footprint, the T10 packs in features. You can run up to 12 mph (a 5:00-mile pace) and incline up to 12%. The 10-inch touchscreen pairs with iFit for trainer-led classes, and the Follow Trainer mode automatically adjusts your incline and speed in real time to match the instructor’s terrain.

SmartAdjust learns your fitness level and tailors your workouts based on how you train, while ActivePulse adjusts intensity based on your heart rate (if paired with a compatible monitor). It’s a smart, sturdy, and space-conscious treadmill that’s ideal for intermediate to advanced runners who want a guided experience at home.

Are you aiming to build muscle like a Greek god or shed those pesky love handles? Different goals call for different equipment. #4927. Nakamoto shares fall 6% premarket after Q3 revenue turns negative

A $5.8 million Bitcoin options loss pushed Nakamoto’s quarterly operating revenue below zero, while the company extended repayment of $60 million in Kraken debt to 2027.

Update (Nov. 13 at 19:04 UTC): This article has been updated to include details of Nakamoto’s amended loan agreement with Kraken.

Shares in Nasdaq-listed Bitcoin treasury company Nakamoto fell 6.5% in premarket trading on Friday after the company reported that losses on Bitcoin options pushed third-quarter operating revenue below zero. Nakamoto also extended the repayment deadline for $60 million in Bitcoin-backed debt owed to Kraken by one year.

Nakamoto’s shares traded at $5.40 at 12:02 pm UTC on Friday, according to Yahoo Finance. At that price, the stock was down about 62% year to date.

Nakamoto reported its third-quarter results after the market closed on Thursday. The company generated $3.9 million in revenue from its businesses. A $5.8 million net loss on Bitcoin options brought total operating revenue to negative $1.9 million, according to its quarterly filing.

Analysts had expected about $17.4 million in revenue, according to estimates compiled by Yahoo Finance.

Nakamoto reported $85.5 million in net income and a $15.8 million adjusted operating loss for the quarter. A $110.4 million gain from revaluing its digital assets, chiefly Bitcoin (BTC), drove the profit. The adjusted operating loss excludes that gain.

Nakamoto held 4,283 BTC worth $357.9 million as of Sept. 30, down from 4,467 BTC at the end of June.

Nakamoto also disclosed that it had extended the repayment deadline for $60 million in Tether USDt (USDT) owed to crypto exchange Kraken by one year, from Dec. 4, 2026, to Dec. 4, 2027, according to an SEC filing.

The amendment leaves the company’s total outstanding debt to Kraken unchanged at 165 million USDT, with the remaining 105 million USDT due June 30, 2027. No principal repayments are scheduled for 2026.

The revised agreement also allows the positive net value of certain Bitcoin derivative positions held with Kraken to count toward collateral requirements, potentially helping Nakamoto offset declines in the value of its pledged Bitcoin before it must provide additional collateral or repay part of the loan.

Nakamoto had pledged 3,030 BTC as collateral at the end of September, representing about 71% of its total holdings, according to its quarterly report.

#4924. Arthur Hayes ‘flattered’ as Coinbase backs US stock perps

Arthur Hayes said he was “flattered” by Coinbase’s defense of US stock perpetual futures, a decade after BitMEX launched perpetual swaps.

Arthur Hayes, co-founder of BitMEX, said he was “flattered” by Coinbase’s support for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) in a US legal dispute over stock perpetual futures.

“When we launched the perpetual swap at BitMEX in 2016, Washington’s reaction was less than warm,” Hayes told Cointelegraph. “Ten years later, Coinbase is in federal court defending the right to offer them on US stocks. I’m flattered. Imitation is the sincerest form of regulation.”

Coinbase and five other companies submitted a brief on Monday opposing the alliance’s request to block trading in perpetual futures tied to individual stocks. The court accepted the brief on Tuesday.

The Capital Markets Alliance Association (CMAA), which brought the lawsuit, says the contracts should be treated as security-based swaps, which face tighter restrictions on retail trading.

Hayes was CEO of BitMEX when the crypto derivatives exchange launched its Bitcoin perpetual swap, which let traders take leveraged positions on Bitcoin without a fixed expiration date. The product helped make perpetual swaps a staple of crypto trading.

The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reportedly submitted a proposed court brief on Monday, opposing the alliance’s request to temporarily halt trading in the contracts.

The agency said it was reviewing the exchanges’ rules for listing the contracts. The brief left open whether the SEC would set those rules aside and whether the contracts qualify as security futures or security-based swaps.

Related: EU DeFi proposals could push users to riskier platforms, says Coinbase exec

In a Tuesday court filing, CMAA said that the CFTC had approved the contracts without adequately explaining its decision or addressing unresolved regulatory questions.

The group also cited about $375 million in reported 24-hour notional trading volume for Kalshi’s stock perpetuals shortly after launch, claiming the products were already diverting business from traditional stock markets.

Stock perpetuals let traders speculate on individual share prices without owning the underlying stocks. Unlike traditional futures, the contracts have no fixed expiration date.

On Nov. 3, US District Judge Valerie Caproni denied the group’s request for a temporary restraining order because it had yet to show likely irreparable harm. She found the alliance was likely to succeed on its claim that the CFTC exceeded its authority.

Wojciech Kaszycki, strategy adviser to BTCS SA, said the lack of a fixed expiration or delivery date could complicate the case for treating perpetual contracts as futures.

Kaszycki told Cointelegraph that the case “sale for future delivery.”

However, he warned that a ruling against the CFTC could push trading activity toward offshore and decentralized platforms.

“The product doesn’t die; it just changes address,” he said.

#4922. Functional Core Workouts Are the Key to Moving Better in and Out of the Gym

Add these 15 expert-approved exercises into your weekly routine.

I don’t know about you, but doing core exercises is my least favorite part of workouts. Unfortunately, though, neglecting functional core training can make a big difference in your total-body strength, and how you move day to day.

Functional training focuses on compound movements that engage multiple muscle groups simultaneously and mimic the way our bodies move during everyday activities. Functionally training the core, specifically, involves strengthening the abdominal muscles that attach to the pelvis or spine.

For instance, a farmer’s carry mirrors the movement of carrying grocery bags. “This is an example of ‘bracing and carrying,’ where you need to keep a tight, braced core to carry the heavy weight,” says Corrine Carnation, CPT, a personal and group trainer at Equinox and creator of the Better You, Better Living program. Plus, a weak core can lead to poor posture and an increased risk of injury.

But the benefits extend way beyond preparing your body for real-life activities and protecting against pain or injury—keep reading for all the reasons you should do functional core movements.

Meet the experts: Corrine Carnation, CPT, is a personal and group trainer at Equinox. Cori Ritchey, CSCS, is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and conditioning coach and group fitness instructor in New York City.

Time: 30 minutes | Equipment (optional): kettlebell, dumbbells, slam ball, resistance band, or Pilates ring | Good for: core, hips, back

Instructions: Choose 5 to 6 exercises from the list below. Complete 2 to 3 sets of the indicated number of reps for each move. Aim to integrate functional core exercises into your training routine once or twice a week.

As these exercises become easier with practice, challenge yourself by increasing resistance while slightly decreasing the number of reps. For example, if 3 sets of 10 reps using bodyweight alone feels easy, try adding a weight or resistance band for 2 or 3 sets of 8 reps. By the last rep of each set, you should feel ready to stop but not completely at failure. When in doubt, start with bodyweight only, then add resistance until you feel the exercise is challenging, but doable.

Pro tip: Exercises aren’t one-size-fits-all, so it’s important to recognize when an exercise is either too challenging, too easy, or not comfortable for you. Keep in mind that every exercise can be modified if needed!

Why it rocks: The suitcase carry prepares the core for real-life activities such as carrying heavy things by your sides. It strengthens the core by making you resist the urge to bend, improving stability and balance—the added grip demand is a fun challenge, too.

1. Holding a weight in one hand, stand up tall and pull your shoulders back and down to prevent them from rolling forward. Keep your core tight and spine neutral.

2. Walk forward for 30 to 60 seconds while maintaining a strong grip and upright posture.

4. Turn around and pick the weight up again, this time with your left hand. Complete 4 reps on each side.

Why it rocks: The halo exercise improves shoulder mobility and stability while strengthening your core. Moving the weight around your head causes a perturbation (or distracting force) to your body, forcing you to stabilize using your core. This particular halo variation has the added benefit of enhancing upper-body strength, targeting the shoulders, back, and arms.

1. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding one dumbbell in front of your chest with both hands and elbows bent at 90 degrees.

2. Slowly circle the dumbbell around your head, moving it clockwise from ear to ear, elbows hugging in.

3. Return to start and repeat the movement counterclockwise. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: Have you ever worried about straining your back when picking something up or twisting? This move strengthens the core, improves stability, and builds rotational strength to protect your body during these movements.

1. Sit on the floor with your knees bent and upper body leaned back until abs are engaged (aim for a 45-degree angle relative to the floor). Hold a slam ball or dumbbell close to your chest with your elbows bent.

2. Keeping your arms slightly bent, twist your torso to the left and slam the ball on the floor next to your left hip.

3. Twist your torso through center to the right and slam the ball on the floor near your right hip. That's 1 rep.

4. Continue alternating for a total of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: The overhead slam exercise requires you to stabilize your body as you lift and forcefully throw the ball down to the floor. It also strengthens your shoulders, arms, and upper back while improving explosive power and coordination.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, a soft bend in knees, and core engaged, while holding a slam ball at your chest with both hands.

2. Rise up tall on your toes and extend your arms overhead holding the slam ball.

3. Bend at your hips (hinging forward slightly) and slam the ball on the floor directly in front of you. Exhale as you throw the ball down toward the floor with force. Be careful not to arch your back.

4. Catch the ball on the bounce while lowering back into the squat position. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: The wood chop exercise helps strengthen your core by working your abs and obliques, which can boost your twisting power and stability, building strength and coordination.

1. Start in a half-kneeling position with your left leg forward and your right leg back, both bent at 90 degrees, holding a dumbbell in front of your chest.

2. With your arms straight, torso upright, and hips facing forward, swiftly lower the weight diagonally across your body to the right hip while twisting to the right. Then, raise the weight to upper left diagonal while twisting to the left. That's 1 rep.

3. Complete 10 reps, then repeat on the other side.

Why it rocks: Keeping your lower back and head flush with the floor while your limbs shift weight will engage your deep core stabilizers. Being able to lift your legs and arms from this position is essential for a healthy spine.

1. Lie faceup holding one dumbbell horizontally in front of your chest with both hands. Lift legs to a tabletop position with your knees over hips, your lower back glued to the floor, and your core engaged.

2. Keeping one leg at a 90-degree angle, lower the other to tap your heel to the floor. As your leg lowers, reach your arms above your head to lower the weight toward the floor behind your head.

3. Engage your core to lift both your arms and leg back to start, then repeat on the opposite side. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise recruits your abdominal muscles to maintain balance and stability. A resistance band offers an added challenge for the core and lower body.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and your hands on your hips or relaxed at your sides. (Optional: Place a resistance band around the arches of both feet.)

2. Balancing on one leg, draw one knee up toward your chest, hold for 1 second, then return it to the floor.

3. Repeat on the opposite side, alternating for 30 seconds. That’s 1 rep.

Why it rocks: Planks help you build the strength to push yourself up from the floor, which is important for many day-to-day activities. Adding the knee drive challenges your upper body and core to stabilize, improving your balance and coordination with uneven movements.

1. Start in a high plank position with your right foot lifted slightly up off the floor.

2. Exhale and pull your right knee toward your chest while rounding the spine to bring your nose toward your knee.

3. With control, reverse movement to return to plank position with right foot lifted. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise challenges you to sit up and lie down without using your hands, which requires strong core muscles. You can do it with a Pilates ring, a ball, or no equipment at all.

1. Lie faceup with your legs slightly bent, heels on floor, and arms extended straight above your head. (Optional: Place a mini resistance band around your wrists for an added challenge.)

2. Engage your core and draw your belly button in as you slowly begin to curl your spine off the mat one vertebra at a time. Roll up to an upright seated position while keeping biceps by the ears and arms reaching to the ceiling.

3. Once you reach the upright position, gradually reverse the movement by slowly rolling back down to the lying position. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise targets the glutes and core, the muscles needed to lift your hips. It's great for anyone who sits a lot, as it both strengthens and mobilizes the hips.

1. Lie faceup with knees bent and feet planted shoulder-width apart on the floor. Place your arms on the floor by your sides or for an added challenge, extend arms above with your hands directly above your shoulders and your palms facing in.

2. Engage your core as you press up into a glute bridge with your knees, hips, and shoulders in alignment, and hold this position.

3. From here, raise your right leg to a 90-degree angle, keeping the stationary leg firmly on the floor and pelvis stable. Return right foot to meet left foot in starting position. That’s 1 rep.

4. Continue alternating legs with your butt lifted and complete 10 to 12 reps on each side.

Why it rocks: The classic side plank targets the obliques, which are essential for stability and rotation in daily activities. It also works your shoulders and hips, promoting good posture and alignment.

1. Lie on your right side with your legs bent, your right elbow directly under your shoulder, and your left hand palm down.

2. Lift your hips off the mat, extending your legs to form a straight line from your head to heels.

3. Hold the position for 30 seconds, then repeat on the opposite side. That’s 1 rep.

Why it rocks: It's similar to the suitcase carry, but levels up the move a bit by testing your stabilization, as you have to stay upright even though the weight is trying to pull you down. Plus, it boosts your grip strength.

1. Stand up straight with feet shoulder-width apart and dumbbell in left hand.

2. Extend your right arm out to the side at a 45-degree angle from your body.

3. Slowly lift your left leg up until knee is at hip height.

4. Then, with control, lower your leg down to the floor. Repeat with right leg. That's 1 rep.

5. Complete 10 to 12 reps, then switch the dumbbell to your right hand.

Why it rocks: It targets your obliques, but also challenges your other core muscles in a more uncommon position. Additionally, it works your spinal mobility.

1. Kneel on left knee with toes pointed to the right, and right foot planted firmly to the side of body, holding a kettlebell in right hand.

2. Rack the kettlebell at chest, then lift it overhead, keeping eyes on the weight.

3. Slowly lower body down until left hand reaches the floor, then continue lowering until elbow and forearm reach the floor.

4. Reverse the movement with control and return to start. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: It's important to train rotation because we're constantly rotating in real life. Plank hip dips strengthen the obliques and stabilize the spine.

1. Start in a forearm plank position with elbows under shoulders and knees, hips, and torso in a straight line.

2. Drop right hip toward the floor, then return to center.

3. Immediately drop the left hip toward the floor.

Why it rocks: This move is one of the best for training functional power, and it demands stabilization from your core.

1. Stand with feet slightly wider than hip-width apart. Hold a kettlebell in front of your body with both hands, arms straight.

2. With a slight bend in the knees and a flat back, hinge at the hips and swing the kettlebell back through the legs. Use that momentum to stand and swing the kettlebell out in front of your body, up to shoulder height.

3. Thrust the hips forward and engage the glutes and core as you stand up straight. When the kettlebell hits shoulder height, the knees should be straight and glutes contracted in a full hip extension.

4. Allow the kettlebell to swing back down through the legs, while hinging at the hips. That's 1 rep.

The best functional core workouts include bodyweight and resistance exercises that challenge the core in different positions and directions. Your core is not one-dimensional, so it’s important to strengthen your body through movements that involve twisting, bending, and stabilizing in all directions. For example, a traditional situp only engages the core in a single plane of motion, but a workout with a Russian twist (for rotational movement), lateral side bends (for side-to-side movement), and plank variations (for multidirectional stability) ensures you are hitting your core muscles from all angles.

Carnation notes the importance of first activating your core before jumping right into a workout. To do so, she recommends the following: “Act as if someone is about to throw a basketball at your stomach.” It might sound odd, but this cue can be really effective in helping you tighten and brace your core to get ready for impact. It’s best to practice this abdominal bracing technique before going into more advanced exercises in order to ensure your core is engaged and ready for action, Carnation says.

#4920. Bitcoin holds below $70K as stocks slip despite a cooler US PPI print

Bitcoin was down about 4% on the day amid a tepid market reaction to October’s US PPI reading, which came in below expected levels.

Bitcoin (BTC) hovered around $68,700 following Friday’s Wall Street open, rebounding from an earlier dip to roughly $67,500.

Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD down 4% on the day after bouncing from a roughly 12-week low near $67,500.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The US Producer Price Index, which tracks changes in the prices domestic producers receive for their goods and services, rose 0.3% month over month and 6.5% year over year in October. Both readings were 0.1 percentage points below market expectations but the annual increase was the largest since November 2022.

“Leading the October advance in final demand prices, the index for final demand goods increased 0.5 percent. Prices for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent,” the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported Friday.

US PPI one-month percentage change. Source: BLS

Stocks showed little sign of relief at the start of the US trading session, with traders still parsing developments around Nvidia after its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned on Thursday.

The S&P 500 was down 1.2% at the time of writing, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index was 1.5% lower.

Nasdaq Composite Index one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The PPI release led markets to slightly adjust expectations for Federal Reserve rate hikes. Odds of a minimal 25-basis-point hike at the Fed’s December meeting rose from 85.4% on Thursday to 89.7%, while odds of a larger 50-basis-point move decreased from 14.5% to 10.3%, per data from CME Group’s FedWatch Tool.

Fed target-rate probability comparison for the December FOMC meeting. Source: CME Group

Economist Robin Brooks described a 25-basis-point hike in December as “all but inevitable.” He argued, however, against a steeper increase, seeing it as ineffective in the face of current inflation drivers: the oil-price spike from the US-Iran war and potential long-term acceleration in underlying inflation.

“If high inflation is about the Strait of Hormuz and oil, 75 basis points won’t do anything about that. If the issue is that the pace of underlying inflation has risen, then 75 basis points is much too timid to get this under control,” he wrote.

Related: Stablecoin supply falls $14.2B in biggest 30-day drop since June 2022

Crypto trader and analyst Rekt Capital warned that a BTC close below $73,000 on Sunday would mark a support breakdown already seen in 2026.

“Last week’s Weekly Candle Closed below 3 Weekly levels,” he wrote on X, referring to $75,000, $76,800 and $78,300. “This Weekly Candle looks set to do something similar. Which is testament to sell-side momentum still gaining and the bears being in control.”

After each of the two previous breakdowns, Bitcoin fell to around $60,000.

BTC/USD one-week chart. Source: Rekt Capital on X.com

At $68,700, BTC/USD is down 17.7% in the fourth quarter and 11.2% month to date. The quarterly performance is currently Bitcoin’s second worst on record, data from CoinGlass confirms.

BTC/USD quarterly returns. Source: CoinGlass

#4919. The 10 Best Face Washes for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Editors

Soaps from Kiehl’s and Tower 28 came out on top in our testing.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

EVERY GOOD SKINCARE routine starts with the same thing—a quality face wash. Before you layer on serums, moisturizers, and eye creams, you need to clear the canvas. A face wash does exactly that by clearing away dirt and grime that accumulate on your skin while also helping prevent clogged pores that can trigger breakouts. That’s why it’s crucial to find the best face wash for you, no matter your skin type.

Wash your face every morning, night, and after heavy workouts to remove bacteria and sebum before they build up, says dermatologistDr. Anthony Rossi, MD. The best face washes for men go beyond cleaning: they hydrate, fight acne, and control excess oil. This first step in your routine is especially important if you live an active lifestyle. While cardio workouts boost circulation and support collagen production, sweat can leave your skin vulnerable to breakouts and irritation.

With so many products out there, finding the right one for your skin type and preferences can feel impossible. That’s why I spent the last two years testing every cleanser I could get my hands on to find the ten best face washes for virtually any skin type and price point.

A face wash is the cornerstone of any skincare routine—without it, the rest of your products won’t work as well. Choose one that’s gentle yet effective because even if your entire routine is just washing your face, you don’t want a cleanser that strips away your skin’s natural oils.

Matching your face wash to your skin type ensures it works with your skin’s natural needs, clears and balances your complexion, and primes your face for the products that follow.

We’ve been testing face washes and cleansers since this story was first published in 2021. As Men's Health's Grooming Editor, I’m also constantly trying out the latest releases to determine which are worth adding to your rotation. For this update, I considered picks from previous iterations of this roundup, as well as current favorites from fellow Men's Health writers and editors. This ultimately led to me testing over 50 face washes, evaluating their ingredients, feel, consistency, and effectiveness. Below is the culmination of this extensive hands-on research: the ten best face washes for men with any skin type or budget.

For active guys who want a no-nonsense soap that still feels luxurious, this cleanser from Kiehl's delivers. Formulated with hydrating glycerin and squalane—and free of parabens and fragrances—it thoroughly cleanses without stripping moisture. Its powerful ingredients clean and hydrate at the same time, leaving your skin soft, balanced, and primed for the rest of your routine.

Testing Notes: I’ve used Kiehl's cleanser for years and love its ultra-smooth formula that glides easily over my skin. I appreciate that it’s fragrance-free, making it ideal for sensitive skin. Lightweight, gentle, moisturizing, and nourishing, it’s one of the most versatile cleansers I’ve tried—perfect for any skin type. At $16 for 2.5 oz, it isn’t the cheapest option, but it’s still on the affordable side of the market. Because it foams so well, I only need a small amount for a full wash, and one container lasts me about two months with daily use. Overall, Kiehl's Ultra Facial Cleanser remains my go-to everyday face wash, no matter your skin type or budget.

This gel cleanser uses zinc, copper, and magnesium to support the skin’s natural defenses while boosting hydration. Aloe vera then locks in moisture and forms a soothing barrier, while oat calms irritation and comforts sensitive skin. Fragrance-free, it gently removes makeup, sunscreen, and daily buildup without stripping or irritating—even for the most reactive skin.

Testing Notes: I don’t have rosacea, but my skin is prone to redness, so I was excited to see this cleanser approved by the National Rosacea Society—and it didn’t disappoint. Whenever my skin flares up, I use it daily, and within a week or two (depending on severity), the redness quickly calms. Its silky consistency also leaves my skin feeling smooth, balanced, and healthy.

You can’t go wrong with a classic. This Cetaphil cleanser, formulated for combination to oily, sensitive skin, actively removes dirt and excess oil while protecting your skin’s natural barrier. The blend of B vitamins and glycerin nourishes as it cleanses, leaving your face refreshed, balanced, and never tight or dry.

Testing Notes: Cetaphil’s Daily Facial Cleanser delivers incredible value for its price. I love that it packs the same hero ingredients you’d see in pricier formulas, like glycerin and niacinamide, yet it’s gentle enough for even ultra-sensitive skin. It leaves my face feeling clean but never stripped, which makes it easy to reach for every day. My only gripe? I wish the pump dispenser worked more smoothly—it can be frustrating when I’m half-asleep and just want a quick wash.

Long before CeraVe went viral on TikTok, grooming experts swore by the drugstore brand for its high-quality ingredients at budget-friendly prices. A perfect example is this cleanser, packed with hydrating staples like hyaluronic acid and ceramides that strengthen the skin barrier while keeping moisture locked in.

Testing Notes: CeraVe’s Facial Cleanser is one of my go-to budget face washes because it’s easy to find online or in stores, and it simply works. I’ve been using CeraVe since my early 20s, and I can honestly say the formula has never let me down—it removes excess oil and grime without ever causing breakouts.

Shaped like a deodorant stick but designed for your face, this solid soap from Oars and Alps packs charcoal, a buzzy exfoliant that gently scrubs without irritation. I love that even a 1.4-oz container lasts over a month when used daily.

Testing Notes: Oars and Alps’ cleansing stick has become my go-to TSA-friendly face soap for traveling and camping. I love how portable it is and how easily it applies—just like my favorite deodorant—while still exfoliating and removing dirt. It easily fits in my Dopp kit, and I don’t need to worry about it leaking or opening. Plus, my face feels incredibly clean after each use, and a little product really does go a long way.

Finding a TSA-friendly cleanser that doesn't spill is hard. That's where Jaxon Lane's Shake and Wake comes in. It's a powder-to-cream product that gently exfoliates skin and cleans just as well as a liquid cleanser, thanks to a powerful combo of niacinamide, vitamin E, and vitamin C. In other words, it's a Dopp kit must-have.

Testing Notes: The first thing I noticed about this wash was its powdery consistency. What surprised me was how much I liked it—and how often I keep reaching for it, especially when traveling. Similar to Oars and Alps Solid Wash, there is minimal risk of spilling—and even if it did (which I’ve yet to experience), the powder will be far less destructive than liquid.

It feels ultra-gentle on my skin and transforms into a soap-like lather as soon as it hits water. The container is TSA-friendly, tightly sealed, and unlikely to leak, and since it’s powder, even a spill would be minimal and far less messy than a gel.

If you're somebody who loves the smell of the great outdoors, or that irreplaceable feeling felt (and smelt) the early morning after a night of camping, then this face wash is for you. Loaded with skin-boosting natural ingredients like aloe vera, caffeine, and charcoal, Dr. Squatch's face wash exfoliates, refreshes, and cleanses with the best of them.

Testing Notes: With its unique charcoal-backed texture and feel, this wash is one of the most rejuvenating options out there. But what really stands out is its understated, yet still attention-grabbing pine tar scent—subtle enough to avoid clashing with your cologne, but woodsy enough to raise the nostrils in the best way possible.

For those with sensitive or dry skin, there are few (if any) better skincare brands than La Roche-Posay. And the brand's cleanser is a perfect representation of why. Its niacinamide-backed formula is equally gentle and hydrating. Add in other moisturizing winners like glycerin, along with the lack of any skin-aggravating ingredients like heavy fragrances or sulfates, and you have one of the lowest risk, highest reward face washes on the market.

Testing Notes: I have sensitive skin and love this cleanser because it never irritates me. Even if your skin is less reactive, the creamy lather feels amazing during and after each wash. It’s gentle and leaves skin feeling hydrated and healthy.

Talk about value—at under $7 a container, it’s hard to find a more effective, affordable face wash for men than Harry’s. Best known for its stellar shave gear, the brand has quietly expanded into no-nonsense men’s skincare, including standouts like its facial moisturizer. This face wash follows the same formula: it packs low-key hydrators like eucalyptus and peppermint alongside gentle exfoliants like glycerin, delivering a no-BS cleanse that gets the job done without breaking the bank.

Testing Notes: Harry’s hasn’t strayed from its facial-hair roots, as this cleanser doubles as one of the best beard washes, softening whiskers and priming them for trimming or shaving. I also can’t overstate how foamy it gets; it not only strips away dirt and buildup but also makes each (already affordable) container last a long time.

Anyone who struggles with acne knows it takes over your routine, demanding protective, non-invasive, blemish-correcting products at every step. For that crucial first cleanse, Geologie’s new Acne Control Face Wash stands out as the best option. Even though it’s been on the market for barely a year, it has already become a staple for me whenever I’m facing a breakout, thanks to its 2 percent salicylic acid formula and silky-smooth application.

Testing Notes: I still reach for this wash whenever I feel a blemish or breakout coming on. The only drawback is that the gel feels a little stringy at first and needs plenty of water before it foams. Once it does, though, the lather expands quickly, and a dime-sized drop covers my entire face—making each bottle last for months.

Wash your face twice a day—morning and night. Just as important, pay attention to the products you use, avoiding harsh chemicals like sulfates and parabens. Choose a gentle cleanser for everyday use and keep an exfoliating scrub for two or three times a week. Apply the scrub with light pressure—fast, hard, and rough isn’t the answer. Overdoing it can damage your skin and create new problems. And always remember: everyone’s skin type is different. What works for one person might not work for another.

#4917. Joseph Dirand Joins Forces with Peter Brant and Stephanie Seymour Brant to Reimagine a Historic 1920s Palm Beach Mansion

It began with a chance encounter and a phone call. The French architect Joseph Dirand was walking into a restaurant in New York when he ran into an old friend, the art dealer Tico Mugrabi. Dirand mentioned that he was flying to Palm Beach the next day and his friend lit up. Mugrabi pulled out his phone and made a call. “Peter, my friend Joseph is coming to Palm Beach tomorrow,” Dirand recalls him saying. “You have to meet this guy.” The following day Dirand was sitting across from Peter Brant, the fabled industrialist and publisher, and his wife, Stephanie Seymour Brant, one of the defining supermodels of her generation, in their new home. The Brants had owned the house for only a few days, and it marked the opening of a new chapter for the couple.

The Brants in front of Warhol’s White Disaster (White Car Crash 19 Times), 1963, in the great room. Jean Prouvé coffee table; sofa and chairs by Pierre Jeanneret.

Marc Newson’s aluminum Lockheed Lounge, a Tower Cabinet by Ettore Sottsass, and a Trapeze table by Jean Prouvé all stand in the loggia.

A Végétale mirror by Claude Lalanne reflects Untitled (Richard Prince and Cindy Sherman), 1980, and a 1930s settee by Jean-Michel Frank.

A pair of bespoke Philippe Anthonioz floor lamps Flank Jonathan Horowitz’s Self-portrait in “Mirror #1” (Kevin), 2012.

Brown Jordan chaise longues under umbrellas by Business & Pleasure Co. stand poolside.

There is something quintessentially American in how quickly it all unfolded, and for Dirand, it meant meeting a man he had long admired. As an inquisitive young designer he had pored over photographs of Brant’s earlier homes, and one image had stayed with him: It showed a Jean Prouvé desk beneath a Jean-Michel Basquiat painting, captured at a time when almost no one thought to set French postwar design against contemporary art. “For me, Peter was a kind of collector’s hero,” says Dirand.

Brant’s eye for art and design was formed early. His father loved classical art and considered even Picasso “way too modern,” but on family ski trips to Switzerland the teenage Brant got to know the Zurich dealer Bruno Bischofberger, who subsequently introduced him to Leo Castelli, and the two titans of the art world became the young Brant’s mentors. Brant then bought his first Andy Warhol painting in 1966, and by the time Warhol’s business manager, Fred Hughes, introduced them in November 1968, he already owned about seven of them. Warhol and Brant would go on to become close friends for the remainder of the artist’s life.

In a corner of the Great Room, Roy Lichtenstein’s The Refrigerator, 1962, faces a 1960 copper hanging cabinet by Paul Evans. a 1934 plaster vase by Alberto Giacometti sits on A Joseph Dirand Edition Iseo Gold coffee table. 1950s Hirondelles wall light by Jean Royère; pair of 1958 Diego Giacometti armchairs.

Warhol’s 1975 portrait of Murray Brant (Brant’s father) commands a wall of the paneled study. Direction armchair and Présidence desk by Jean Prouvé; Ettore Sottsass hanging lamp.

Artworks in the entrance hall include, from left, a Massangis stone lion-head fountain feature by Harumi Klossowska de Rola, 2022; Andy Warhol’s Self Portrait (Green), 1964; a Klossowska de Rola wolf sculpture; and Richard Prince’s Nurses’ Dormitory, 2002. The sanded Ceppo di Gré stone modular console is by Dirand.

In the primary bedroom, George Condo’s 2004 portrait of Stephanie Seymour Brant hangs above a 1946 Charlotte Perriand sideboard on which stands an enameled earthenware lamp by Roger Capron. A Jean Prouvé Bridge armchair joins an Ours Polaire chair and sofa by Jean Royère around Prouvé’s Tripod coffee table.

An exterior view of the 1926 Addison Mizner residence

Few people then saw Warhol’s work the way Brant did. When he hung his first Marilyn at home, visitors were shocked: “People would come to my house and think, This is the worst thing I’ve ever seen. In the 1960s, he says, you could count the serious collectors of Pop art “on three hands.”

His rule, he says, is to collect “something that was in style that’s out of style,” though never as speculation. Between their holdings and those of the Brant Foundation, which he established in 1996 to promote the education and appreciation of contemporary art and design, the collection now numbers more than 3,000 works, and he has never bought for a particular wall. What he misses in many newer collections is any sense of the person behind them. “You can see right away that this guy had a great adviser,” he says, “but there’s no madness in the collection. Every collection should have some madness.”

Carlo Mollino’s Tipo B side chair rests beneath Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Per Capita, 1981.

A painting by Glenn Ligon and a stool by Shiro Kuramata in Brant’s bath

Seymour Brant and Brant in the great room

Brant has shared much of his collecting journey with Seymour Brant, whom he married in 1995. She has built a collection of her own: Her passion is clothing rather than paintings, and she has pursued it with the same scholarship and the same sharp eye as her husband. She was a close friend of the legendary couturier Azzedine Alaïa and has one of the most significant holdings of his work, alongside historic couture that Dirand describes as extraordinary. Where Brant is the storyteller, Seymour Brant is the quieter presence, though Dirand is clear that she was integral to every decision. Her collecting has even changed the way Brant sees his own. “It’s not a dress in a closet,” he says. “It’s a piece of art, and it mixes with art.”

Brant has spent some 50 years in the Palm Beach area, first as a polo player. He and Seymour Brant had no need for a new home there—they loved the one they had as their children grew up. But when Collado Hueco, a home by Addison Mizner, the architect who defined 1920s Palm Beach, came on the market in 2020, the collector in him took over. “It was a piece of history,” Dirand says. “For him, there was no choice.” Designed in 1924 for the American businessman Paul Moore, it is one of Mizner’s boldest and most unusual houses.

In a hall, a 1974 Diego Giacometti bench sits in front of Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Untitled (Sugar Ray Robinson), 1982. The curtain rods are by Julian Schnabel.

Warhol’s The Kiss (Bela Lugosi), 1964, and a 1947 Alexandre Noll mahogany armchair in a corner of the primary bedroom. Philippe Anthonioz hanging light; Jean Prouvé tripod coffee table; Jean Royère Ours Polaire sofa.

John Currin’s Constance Towers, 2009, presides over Seymour Brant’s dressing room. Furniture includes an Ambassador chair and Éléphanteau sofa, both by Jean Royère.

In the great room, a plaster bas-relief, Support, and a carved-stone console by Alberto Giacometti are flanked by a pair of Éléphanteau chairs by Jean Royère. In the foreground is a Fondation Maeght chair by Diego Giacometti.

The house presented Dirand with a real puzzle. Asymmetrical, it spreads across multiple wings, varying from one to three levels. The main entertaining rooms had retained their original character, while the entrance and stair hall were dark and enclosed. Dirand set out to let the sunlight that moves across the house reach every part of the interior as much as possible. The collection shaped Dirand’s approach too. With so many treasured works coming into the house, the team wanted to ensure they would be protected against anything the unpredictable Florida weather could bring. What began as a renovation became, in Dirand’s words, “a reconstruction saving the historical.” Rather than demolishing and starting again, the team kept the historic walls standing, reinforced every one of them, and dug beneath to take the foundations deeper. New hurricane-proof windows were set into concrete frames, the roof was removed and rebuilt, and the original tiles and the patina of the plaster fireplace were carefully preserved. The project took about four years. Throughout, Dirand immersed himself in Mizner’s doors, ceilings, and patterns so that the new rooms would be a true homage rather than a copy.

Early on, Brant handed Dirand two thick binders, one of artworks and one of design pieces. “This is what you can use,” he said. A few days later, on holiday with his family, Dirand spread every page across the floors. “I was walking on the paper,” he says. It reversed the usual order in which the architect designs the rooms and the art arrives afterward. Here the collection came first, though never rigidly, because “a collection is also something that is alive.”

A Diego Giacometti bench and A Jean Royère Liane six-branch floor lamp in a hall

A chair and floor lamp by Diego Giacometti stand next to the fireplace in the great room.

Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Per Capita, 1981, commands a wall of the loggia. Ours Polaire chair and Yo-Yo side table, both by Royère.

A family photo and fragrance bottles line up on a windowsill in Seymour Brant’s bath.

Warhol’s Big Campbell’s Soup Can with Can Opener (Vegetable), 1962, hangs in the stairwell, which also features a Jacques Adnet wall light.

At the heart of the home are two main spaces, the great room and the loggia, which are perhaps the spaces that both Dirand and Brant are most proud of. The great room is centered around a monumental fireplace that has the grandeur of a castle. Commanding one wall is a rare carved-stone console by Alberto Giacometti, nearly three meters high and crowned with a bas-relief of a female figure, made for Jean-Michel Frank’s important 1938 commission for the Born family in Argentina. It was one of a pair, and Dirand says no one knows where the other is today. Beside the fireplace hangs Warhol’s 1963 White Disaster (White Car Crash 19 Times), one of Brant’s most recent and important acquisitions; he had wanted a Car Crash painting since the ’60s. Prouvé furniture from Brazzaville, weathered by the Congo climate, sits amid Native American and African objects, and at the center of it all is a mirror polish copper table Dirand designed himself to reflect Giacometti’s bird vase and the fireplace behind it. Brant calls the table a masterpiece.

Art in the main entrance includes, from left, pieces by Jean-Michel Basquiat, Richard Prince and Cindy Sherman, and Brice Marden. Furniture includes an Ours Polaire Chair and sofa and a kidney-shaped coffee table, all by Jean Royère, and a Charlotte Perriand stool. a 1936 Jean-Michel Frank settee stands in the background.

A glimpse into the primary bedroom, where a Jean-Michel Frank table lamp sits atop a bedside table.

A wall niche holds a 2023 ibis sculpture by Harumi Klossowska de Rola

The loggia is lighter and more playful, and its original black, yellow, and turquoise tiled floor and Egyptian-style column capitals offer a glimpse of Mizner at his most adventurous. One of the most prominent works hanging in the room is a monumental 1981 Basquiat painting, Per Capita, which Brant bought from Annina Nosei’s memorial show for the artist. At the center of the room stands an Ettore Sottsass Tower Cabinet, designed in the early 1960s, which Dirand admits he didn’t understand at first, until Brant showed him exactly how to place it. Now he can’t imagine the room without it.

Upstairs, Dirand took down walls so that the primary bedroom runs the full width of the house, capturing light from sunrise over the ocean to sunset over the garden. In Seymour Brant’s bathroom, Estremoz marble walls are carved to evoke curtains, and beyond it lies her dressing room, an intimate boudoir. Brant’s bathroom, by contrast, is a marquetry of white and gray marble built around a pair of Glenn Ligon paintings. Dirand calls the room “minimalist ornamental.”

A 2023 flamingo sculpture by Harumi Klossowska de Rola (one of a pair) stands on the terrace.

In Seymour Brant’s bath, François-Xavier Lalanne’s Singe II, 1999, sits between a stool by Diego Giacometti and a bespoke bench by Philippe Anthonioz.

Every piece in the house comes with a story, and Dirand heard many of them over years of breakfasts, lunches, and dinners with the couple. “Every single piece could be a book,” he says. During those conversations, the collaboration between Brant and Dirand grew into a close friendship. Brant’s other great passion is horse racing, and his formidable stable has included Sottsass, the 2020 winner of the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe, Europe’s most prestigious race. One day, Brant called Dirand with news: Sottsass had a son, a young thoroughbred already winning races of his own. He had named him Dirand.

#4916. Metaplanet swings to $170M loss as Bitcoin sale hits earnings

Bitcoin sales, valuation losses and rising borrowing costs weighed on the Japanese company’s earnings despite higher revenue and operating profit.

Metaplanet swung to a $170 million net loss in the first nine months of 2026, hit by a decline in the value of its Bitcoin holdings and a loss on the sale of 10,000 coins to demonstrate its ability to raise cash.

The Japanese company, the world’s second-largest publicly traded corporate Bitcoin (BTC) holder, posted a net loss of 27.16 billion yen (about $170 million), compared with a profit of 13.53 billion yen ($84.6 million) in the same period last year. A 19.17 billion yen ($119.8 million) loss on the Bitcoin sale and an 8.04 billion yen ($50.3 million) loss from a decline in the value of its Bitcoin holdings outweighed gains in the operating business.

Over the quarter, Metaplanet sold the 10,000 BTC for 124.7 billion yen and temporarily held the proceeds in cash, stablecoins and other liquid assets. It then spent 149.9 billion yen to buy 11,000 BTC, paying 9.3% more per coin on average. The company said the sale was meant to show rating agencies and bond investors that it could turn its Bitcoin into cash to meet financing obligations. At the end of September, holdings rose by a net 1,000 coins to 44,000 BTC.

Top 10 largest Bitcoin treasury companies. Source: BitcoinTreasuries.NET

Metaplanet borrowed against its Bitcoin holdings during the quarter, increasing the amount it owed under the credit line to $649.5 million at the end of September from $414 million at the end of June.

The company said it funded Bitcoin purchases from the second quarter onward with money borrowed under the credit line, proceeds from bond sales and the exercise of stock acquisition rights, and revenue from its Bitcoin options business.

Metaplanet’s interest expense rose 56% from the previous quarter to 1.36 billion yen ($8.5 million). Short-term borrowings and bonds payable totaled 110.5 billion yen ($691 million) at the end of September.

For the nine months through September, revenue rose 30.5% to 5.9 billion yen ($36.9 million), while operating profit increased 26.5% to 3.48 billion yen ($21.8 million). The company cut its full-year revenue forecast to 6.5 billion yen ($40.6 million) from 16 billion yen ($100 million).

Related: Metaplanet to take 93.7% stake in Super League through 2,100 BTC deal

Metaplanet’s earnings come as Bitcoin treasury companies face mounting pressure from incoming stock index removals and falling Bitcoin prices.

Index provider MSCI confirmed Wednesday that Strategy, Metaplanet and Upexi would be removed from its equity indexes at the Nov. 30 market close, potentially prompting funds that track those benchmarks to sell the shares. JPMorgan previously estimated that Strategy’s removal could result in roughly $2.8 billion in selling pressure from MSCI-linked funds.

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday and was trading around $68,600 as of 4:51 p.m. UTC, down about 9% over the previous week, according to CoinGecko data.

Supplements are unregulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)—and that includes creatine. As such, experts say it’s important to consider the following factors and complete your due diligence to find a high-quality product when shopping for a creatine supp. (Reading this article counts!)

Simplicity is often best with creatine. Look for products that list creatine as the sole active ingredient, ideally without added sugars, unless you're choosing a flavored version intentionally. Avoid proprietary blends that don’t disclose exact creatine content per serving.

The recommended daily dose of creatine is a minimum of five grams per day, according to the International Society of Sports Nutrition. This amount is shown to be safe and effective for maintaining creatine saturation within the muscles.

There are several types of creatine available, including monohydrate, citrate, and nitrate, but creatine monohydrate remains the most reliable. It’s the most extensively researched, dependable, effective, and cost-efficient option.

The U.S. supplement industry is largely unregulated, which means that the FDA doesn’t verify supplement marketing claims before products hit the shelves. But third-party testing can help. Look for certifications from organizations like Informed Choice or NSF Certified for Sport, which ensure the product has been tested for purity, potency, and contaminants. This is especially critical for competitive athletes concerned about banned substances.

For most people, taking creatine daily is not only okay, but it’s actually recommended to maintain optimal muscle creatine levels. Consistent daily use supports better performance, recovery, and long-term benefits.

The most common side effect of creatine is short-term water retention, which can lead to temporary weight gain. Taking more than 10 grams at once may also cause digestive issues such as bloating or diarrhea. However, for most people, creatine is well-tolerated when used as directed.

If you have pre-existing kidney or liver conditions, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or are a child or adolescent, it’s important to consult your healthcare provider before taking creatine. For most healthy adults, creatine is safe and effective, but checking in with your doctor can provide added peace of mind and guidance.

#4914. US regulators move ahead on crypto trust charters as Senate scrutiny grows

Coinbase’s trust company received final clearance as lawmakers seek records on crypto firms’ compliance and potential conflicts of interest.

Federal regulators are opening more avenues for crypto companies to operate under US rules, while congressional investigators are asking to see the records behind those decisions. Lawmakers want to know how regulators justified new trust charters, how crypto companies handled compliance and what dealings they had with people tied to President Donald Trump’s administration.

On Nov. 9, Coinbase announced that its national trust company had received final approval to open. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted preliminary conditional approval in April. The company said the charter gives its custody business a consistent federal framework.

Lawmakers had been questioning how federal regulators were using their existing authority to expand crypto companies’ reach. In a May 18 letter to the OCC, Sen. Elizabeth Warren challenged at least nine crypto trust-charter approvals, including Coinbase’s earlier conditional approval. She asked for the applications, the legal analyses behind the approvals and any related communications between OCC officials and the White House or Trump family.

Four days before Coinbase’s announcement, Sen. Richard Blumenthal renewed demands for records from Binance, Tether and two Trump-linked ventures. He gave them until Jan. 4, 2027, to turn over the requested records voluntarily and warned that his subcommittee could take other steps to obtain them.

We also took into account price, as some basketball goals provide a better overall value than others.

In addition, we also consulted world-renowned basketball shooting coach Chris Matthews (a.k.a. Lethal Shooter) on what makes for a good portable hoop. Our guide below represents our top picks, all approved by Matthews, of portable basketball hoops that will actually last for years to come. Keep scrolling to learn more.

Not every hoop is going to have the same adjustability in terms of how low or high you can raise it. This is crucial if you have little ones and want the whole family to partake in the fun. It’s also a great way to put on a dunk contest if you still have the bunnies, too. There are also different mechanisms built for adjusting, such as a hand crank, a telescoping pole, pneumatic assist, or a gas spring.

The types of materials used directly impact the long-term durability of your hoop. The two types of backboard materials to know about for portable basketball goals are acrylic and polycarbonate (there's also glass, but glass is used for professional backboards and is extremely rare on portable ones). Polycarbonate is going to be cheaper, but the tradeoff is that exposure to weather and UV light will make the backboard brittle and rigid over time. Acrylic is typically more expensive, but the benefit is that it's better suited for exposure to weather and UV light (acrylic is not affected by UV light like polycarbonate), plus you get a more responsive bounce.

Basketball rims are not all created equal. If you’ve ever been to a park court, you know what we mean—one slightly off shot and your ball rockets across the street. There are a few common materials you’ll see: steel and double-rimmed steel, powder-coated rims, and occasionally composite or plastic. You’ll also see that there are breakaway rims, standard, and flex.

To keep a portable basketball hoop in place, you'll need to fill its base with something. Most portable goals hold about 35 gallons, and you can either go with water or sand. We prefer sand because it dissipates well. Sand is also denser than water, so filling the base with sand is wiser for a more secure hold. However, choosing water makes it easier to empty the base and refill, making it easier to maneuver, especially if you need to move elsewhere in your driveway (or take it to your neighbor's for a friendly pickup game).

If you're curious about how much weight you need to keep your goal in place, a safe number is around 300 to 450 pounds. It sounds like a lot, but if you want to be safe and protect your goal, then more weight is always worth adding. And keep in mind that they all include wheels attached to the base to move them more easily. If you want to eliminate the labor of filling the base full, you can fill it to a point and then stack sandbags on top of the back of the goal to keep it in place. It won't be the most pleasing to look at, but it will allow you to move the goal around more easily.

Paying more gets you a better playing experience, especially when it comes to a wide acrylic backboard. A wider backboard makes it easier to shoot bank shots and perform layups, and the acrylic material will be much more responsive and last longer. A more expensive goal might also come with better wheels for moving the goal. Keep in mind a portable basketball hoop won't be as deluxe as an in-ground one, but you can get pretty dang close.

A regulation backboard is typically 48 inches tall by 72 inches wide. Most portable hoops have a 48-inch height, but there's a variance on width. While 72 inches is fun to play on due to the full ability to shoot bank shots and layups, a driveway goal doesn't need to be that wide.

Look to a 50-inch or 54-inch width. Anything under 50 is fine; however, you will lose space to shoot bank shots and layups. The benefit to buying a goal with a smaller backboard, though, is that you save money (they're almost always cheaper).

The easiest way to store a portable basketball goal is to lower the rim to its lowest setting, tarp it, then roll it into a garage or shed. Some basketball hoops can be disassembled (or at least partially disassembled), but that process can be pretty annoying. Make sure to drain any water from the base to avoid it freezing and expanding the plastic of the base.

Some of the high-end Spalding portable goals can partially disassemble for storage (not the Spalding EZ we recommend, though). You can take out bolts at the middle of the goal, and the backboard will fold down, thus helping store it in a garage or shed with a low ceiling.

Jeff Turbett is a fitness and wellness writer who's based in Miami, FL. His work has been featured in The Manual and FightCamp.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.
