#4911. How One Creative Couple Found Harmony in Their 1920s Los Angeles Craftsman

Nothing about where interior designer Harrison Soll is now was part of the plan. Five years ago, he was focused on his work, and he didn’t want any distractions. But when he met Rodney Burns, a stylist and owner of the legendary Los Angeles vintage gallery, Church Boutique, it set everything on a new path. They met in the fall; by New Year’s they were a couple. “I didn’t think it was going to be a relationship,” Soll says. He credits their shared interests for bringing them together: “We always found a throughline with design.”

They now live in a 1925 craftsman house in Laurel Canyon. Soll took the lead decorating the nearly 1,400-square-foot home in a combination of his and Burns’s styles with many pieces coming from Burns’s eclectic collection of vintage art, furniture, and sculpture. Burns has worked with Lenny Kravitz as a stylist and creative collaborator for the past 15 years, and the singer says he admires what Burns and Soll have created together. “The mix of Rodney’s early- to midcentury style mixed with ethnic expression next to Harrison’s bold minimalist modern approach seamlessly blend together,” Kravitz tells AD.

The backyard of Soll’s and Burns’s Laurel Canyon home is a bricolage of funky, inherited stonework and vintage pottery.

The nail art above the fireplace has a cute backstory story: Burns and Soll had seen it at a vintage shop in Santa Monica and Burns regretted not buying it. When he went back to purchase the piece, it was marked as sold. But only because Soll had already covertly bought it as a Valentine’s Day gift for Burns.

The giant Sergio Bustamante giraffe bust in the foyer is a delicate topic. “The giraffe was one of our biggest fights in decorating this house,” Burns explains. “I was determined to have that giraffe live some place in this house because he’s just fantastic, and the scale of him, and the rarity of him.” Except, counters Soll, that the placement of the giraffe is treacherous because the front door swings right in its path. “You just have to be careful,” Soll says.

The foyer—which features a collection of masks and vintage paintings—was one of the most difficult areas to style, explains Burns. The couple was trying to be selective of what pieces to incorporate from Burns’s massive collection and at one point Burns suggested putting all of his masks in storage to save for another house down the line, or passing them onto Burns’s vintage boutique, Church. Soll dissented, saying, “No, let’s put them everywhere.”

The living room features two sofas—a Joseph D’Urso for Knoll piece reupholstered in leopard fabric and a leather De Sede Terrazza. The carpet is the Antilocarpa style from Stark. A trio of fiberglass shell art was sourced through Kelly Wearstler. The art behind the sofa is a manipulated canvas garment bag by the artist Roosevelt “Rip” Woods, the first black artist to have a solo show at the Phoenix Art Museum.

As renters, there were naturally limitations on what could be achieved. Soll got permission to retile a bathroom and install a new vanity. The doe-patterned wall-to-wall carpeting in the living room was an “ask for forgiveness” move, but his landladies ended up loving it. Burns, on the other hand, needed more convincing. “The carpet took many dinners of conversations between the two of us,” Soll says.

Soll describes himself as more of a minimalist while Burns avows, “I’m a maximalist to the umpteenth power.” The couple attempted to strike a balance while still filling the space with character. Some rooms nod to Soll’s leanings toward minimalism like an office with a midcentury desk and a 1970s tapestry and the dining room where a Sergio Bustamante table and a Chinese Art Deco rug are the main attractions.

When decorating their Laurel Canyon home, Soll and Burns had to figure out how to combine their opposing styles, with Soll being more of a minimalist and Burns being a maximalist. But, says Burns, “[Soll] has made me be able to take a pause and then also make me a little less attached to some of the things that I’ve collected  and given me an opportunity to maybe show a little bit more restraint.” In the corner, a brass Maison Jansen palm tree mingles with a Sergio Bustamante monkey.

Burns, who has been styling Lenny Kravitz for over a decade, says his approach to home design and fashion are one in the same: “Building an outfit, building a room: same thing in my opinion.”

Kravitz offers these kind words on Burns: “What I love about Rodney is that he is limitless in his concepts and always thinks outside of the box. His visual vocabulary enables him to mix a vast stew of eras and genres. He pays tribute to our ancestors and uplifts new innovators. Always soulful, expressive, and elegant.”

In the dining room, Soll placed a Sergio Bustamante table on a diagonal to make enough room for the couple’s large dog. “She’s a girthy girl,” says Soll, referring to the table, not the dog. The chairs are by Paul Evans and the Chinese Art Deco rug was sourced from Ariana Rugs. The Tom Greene chandelier was sourced from Burns’s boutique, Church.

Burns’s maximalism is on display in the living room, where a couch upholstered in leopard Scalamandré mixes with zebra-hide chairs and a sinuous De Sede sofa. (That animal print couch, Soll wants you to know, also features a block of leather upholstery: “I just think it would have been too maximalist to do a full Scalamandré sofa.”)

The living room is filled with brass sculptures (a Maison Jansen palm tree and a Sergio Bustamante monkey), bronze figures sourced from an estate sale in Arizona, and several pieces of sculptural artwork.

The bedroom mixes patterns and textures with a stainless steel bed from TTMM, Paul Evans “Cityscape” nightstands, striped bedding, and antique bronze table lamps with African mud cloth shades.

The 1970s textile art in the office is a vintage find of Burns’s that Soll loves. “I used to go to Rodney’s apartment when we first started dating, and I would be like, ‘Oh my God! Like, if we break up, I’m never gonna be able to find this tapestry,’” he says.

Soll got permission from his landladies to retile the bathroom and add a new vanity. The metal Curtis Jeré artwork comes from Burns’s collection.

The bohemian architecture of the home lends quirkiness to the design. The main bedroom isn’t a perfect square, making it seem like a stainless steel bed from TTMM is placed on a diagonal but is actually following the geometry of a very funky, angular bedroom.

The couple has taken their time tinkering and adjusting the decor, taking a considered approach to collecting and combining their belongings. Soll describes the overall vibe as having an Afrocentric theme that’s also a little bit Ralph Lauren. “Our visions have mingled,” Burns says.

Still, there is one last item the couple needs to complete the design: a blanket basket. But, says Soll, “We still haven’t found one we agree upon.”

The backyard is also home to a shed (not pictured), which functions as Burns’s closet.

#4910. Want Studio-Style Pilates at Home? Start With These Editor-Tested Reformers

Our top picks for every kind of at-home Pilates setup, from compact machines to studio-worthy reformers.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a pilates princess, you already know what a reformer is, and you’re well acquainted with the many ways it delivers a low-impact, strength-building workout. However, if you’re a newbie, here’s a quick crash course: A reformer is a specially designed machine, originally developed by Joseph Pilates, that consists of springs for resistance, a moving carriage, a foot bar that you push or pull, and pulleys to hold onto or hook to your feet when performing pilates exercises.

“I’d describe the reformer as a machine designed to help create an understanding of your body with resistance,” says Sam Miles, owner and co-founder of Good Time Pilates in New York City. “It gives real time feedback so you can find sensation through the shortening and lengthening of your muscles. In short and easy terms: an assist to finding your muscle engagement!”

There are unique benefits to using a reformer that are hard to replicate in a pilates mat workout, or really any other type of workout. But that doesn’t mean you have to be advanced to start using one. “The modifications to increase or decrease challenge make it a truly universal machine for any body and any fitness level, which is very unique and just awesome,” Miles says. “You can rehabilitate with a reformer, strengthen muscles, stretch and find release work, it’s the best!”

Pilates reformers are available in different types: classical and contemporary. The classical reformer stays true to Joseph Pilates’ original design; the machines are made of wood, and have springs that all have the exact same resistance level. Purists are going to want to consider these machines.

Contemporary reformers are an evolutionary riff on the original and often incorporate springs of varying resistance that can be adjusted. The dimensions also usually vary a bit from the OG classical reformer design.

While it used to be that reformers were only found in Pilates studios, more and more women are investing in a reformer as an addition to their home gym setup. There are also less intense reformer models on the market that are specifically designed for at-home use, and these generally come in at a fraction of the cost of a classical or studio-grade contemporary reformer.

After testing a bunch of options, we narrowed down our picks to a variety of machines, including commercial-grade reformers and pared-down, reimagined reformers that are made specifically to take up less space and be more affordable.

After testing a handful of Pilates reformers, the contemporary-style Balanced Body Allegro 2 came out on top for its studio-quality, strong springs, durable build, and versatile foot bar. WH fitness contributor Talene Appleton has been using it two to three times a week to practice at home for almost two years, and it’s still in mint condition. Appleton says it’s built like a tank and is commercial-grade, so it’s the best you can get for your at-home gym setup.

Five springs are featured for varying tension to accommodate different levels—three high resistance (red), one medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow), while the steel, grippy foot bar glides effortlessly for 10 vertical and horizontal positions. “I was blown away by how much the additional positions of its foot bar allowed me to change up my usual Pilates sequences,” says Appleton. “This adds incredible versatility in terms of movement options that most competitors can’t beat.” While the foot bar is its best feature, Appleton notes it’s the most difficult to set up and requires two people to line it up evenly on each side.Appleton says this machine is best for advanced users, given there’s a bit of a learning curve at first. “Using a traditional reformer at home can be a bit overwhelming at first, especially if you’re used to having an instructor call the shots in terms of spring resistance, foot bar positions, moves, and all the rest,” she says. “I found myself second-guessing my setup and wondering if I was getting the most out of each exercise (or sometimes if the move I was doing was even a real exercise at all).” She credits YouTube and TikTok tutorials for guiding her along, specifically from Balanced Body and East River Pilates.While this is the best Pilates machine money can buy (with a steep price tag of $4,345 *sigh*) it’s heavy at 157 pounds. It’s also large, at eight feet long and three feet wide, so make sure you have adequate space before splurging. It’s also not the easiest to set up. “Setting this thing up was no joke—I knew I was in for a challenge when I saw the multiple massive, heavy boxes it arrived in,” Appleton says. She notes it took her and a friend two hours to assemble.

Read More: Balanced Body Allegro 2 Review

The classical Merrithew At Home SPX Reformer is next-level if you want to up your Pilates game. It features a foldable vertical tower, which can improve flexibility and target different muscle groups with more controlled movements, adding more challenge. It has five springs—four full-resistance and one with half-resistance. Given the springs mostly have the same resistance, this machine is designed for more advanced users.

The foot bar is adjustable with four positions for different heights, while the carriage is padded for comfort. Another call-out is the included reformer box, which adds height and range of motion to moves in the seated and lying position. It’s especially helpful for those with muscle tightness or who need to modify moves involving the knees.

While this is a great reformer to elevate your practice, it’s quite large at 96 inches long and 26 inches wide. It’s also heavy at 115 pounds. Like the AeroPilates Pro XP 557, this isn’t ideal for apartments. The tower structure also requires more vertical space, so if you don’t have high ceilings, our best overall is most likely your best bet.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment

Pretty much all pilates reformers in this guide are relatively large, but the contemporary AeroPilates Reformer 4420 is foldable. If you’re an apartment dweller, this machine is your compact answer to your Pilates reformer dreams. It can be stashed under a couch, bed, or behind a door. At 69 pounds, it’s not the lightest, so having two people for setup is probably your best bet.

Like the AeroPilates Reformer 287, it uses cords, not springs, yet delivers impressive effectiveness. This model has four adjustable cords with varying resistances and color codes, unlike the 287: two standard resistances (black), one extra intensity (red), and one light resistance (yellow). So, this reformer is good for both beginners and those who are more advanced.

It also has a built-in cardio rebounder, which is essentially a mini trampoline at the foot bar, making it an especially good choice for someone looking for low-impact cardio options and variety.

The contemporary Your Reformer is studio-grade like our best overall reformer pick, and is super durable despite being a little over half the price. During a stay in Los Angeles, Appleton rented one for at-home workouts and was extremely impressed with its easily changeable five thick springs, and a carriage that glides smoothly and quietly. The springs are also color-coded: two heavy resistance (red), two medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow).

In terms of quality, it’s a direct competitor to the Allegro 2. “The straps are thick and definitely won’t fray on me, and the strap handles are comfortable to grip, even when my palms get sweaty,” Appleton says. It’s not compact enough for most apartments, but it’s slimmer to accommodate home spaces better.

Appleton is 5’5” and found the carriage to be wide and spacious, with plenty of room to move around from supine to standing to kneeling positions. It also accommodates her much taller boyfriend, who’s “20 times more passionate about a good reformer workout,” so it’s the real deal.

The AeroPilates Reformer 287 is the most affordable option we’ve come across. It’s dramatically less expensive than our best overall—it costs under $400! But that doesn’t mean it’s less effective. Its quality is still impressive, just not studio-grade. WH entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson, an avid Pilates practitioner, was surprised by how sturdy this machine is because of its bargain price, and since it comes pre-assembled (another plus).

But, she stresses it’s best for beginners since it only features three resistance cords. “I could see someone eventually progressing beyond the capabilities of this model, especially when it comes to exercises like footwork and running, which are classically done on four springs,” says Wilkinson. “It also lacks certain accessories you’d typically find with a studio machine—a box, which is typically used for exercises in the short-box series and in a long position for pulling straps and T-press, among others.”

Speaking of resistance, unlike our best overall, this reformer uses cords instead of springs. While they can be trickier to hook on and off, their weight is identical to springs Wilkinson uses on studio-grade models.The carriage glides smoothly, although Wilkinson notes the attached handles would fall and get in the way. She recommends tossing them aside instead of hanging on the built-in shoulder blocks. As for the foot bar, it’s stable but can’t be adjusted for specific exercises.Aside from mechanics, this reformer is extremely compact, weighing just 56 pounds, and measuring 42 inches when folded and 85 inches fully extended. Wilkinson lives in a one-bedroom Brooklyn apartment and has no issues stashing it away, although she finds it tricky to fold and wide when the foot bar is attached.AeroPilates says this product can fit people up to 6'4", but Wilkinson, who is 5’11”, says even her height was pushing the machine’s limits. “I imagine anyone much taller than I am would feel a bit crunched,” she says. She also says it’s narrow, and didn’t have additional breathing room.

While most full-sized pilates reformers don’t have a built-in trampoline at the foot bar, the contemporary AeroPilates Pro XP 557 is the first full-sized model we’ve seen with a rebounder, so cardio moves like single-leg pushups and slow squats can be added to the routine. This is especially useful for beginners getting into the groove. WH associate visual editor Berkeley Brooks found it stayed sturdy when executing explosive movements at fast paces, while the material of the main carriage prevented her from slipping around.

Brooks notes that the four strong springs are easily interchangeable and have varying resistances labeled by color: two low resistance (blue) and two high resistance (yellow). The foot bar is adjustable, thick, and quiet for added comfort, and can be placed in three positions to accommodate different heights without disrupting your range of motion.

The platform is also wide at 23 inches and long at 100 inches, so this model isn’t ideal for small apartments, especially since you need additional space to execute exercises.

On the upside, Brooks says it’s easy to build and aesthetically pleasing. “I love the addition of wood to the machine because it looks great in a home gym,” she adds.

The springs in a pilates reformer are an important consideration when you’re choosing your machine. “Springs provide resistance and feedback, so the type and responsiveness of springs deeply influence your experience,” says Mo Wolfe, owner and Pilates instructor of Evolution Pilates in Port Washington, New York.

The weight of springs can also depend on whether a machine is classical or contemporary. Classical style reformers have a heavier spring tension that is the same throughout, while modern models generally tend to offer springs with a variety of resistance levels. A reformer with springs is the type you’ll find in a Pilates studio.

Alternatively, resistance cords are sometimes used in the place of springs in reformer machines that are designed for personal and at-home use. They offer similar effectiveness and are more affordable.

Taking the size of your home into consideration is important before purchasing a Pilates machine. Not only do you want to make sure you have enough room for the machine itself, you also want to make sure there will be enough space to perform the full range of Pilates reformer exercises, like leg circles, that require room to move.

Some reformers are very big and bulky, such as our pro-level, best overall selection. They take up considerable real estate and they’re best for a home gym where they can become a more permanent fixture that won’t need to be moved once it’s installed.

If your workout space is multi-functional (i.e., it’s your living room) and your equipment needs to have a smaller footprint and be more portable so you can move it around or stash it away, look for a lighter, foldable option. Just make sure that you’ll have enough space to do the moves when it’s all set up.

Since reformer Pilates is a low-impact activity, and the resistance can be so fine-tuned for your fitness level, there are no hard and fast rules about how often you do a reformer session each week. Miles says it really comes down to how your body feels. “With the variety you can get from a reformer, daily use is manageable. At my studio we have challenging classes, stretch and release classes, technique-focused classes; variety is important!” She notes that most of her clients do three reformer sessions per week.

We picked the brains of Pilates instructors to understand what to look for when shopping for a reformer, then researched dozens of the top-rated models. From there, Women’s Health writers and editors (including fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, and entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson) tested some of the best themselves to narrow down the options.

During testing, they paid close attention to spring and cord resistance level as a measure of whether or not the machines were ideal for beginners or more advanced users. The testers also considered size, durability, and ease of assembly to determine what sorts of spaces were needed for these machiness. Moves like planks, triceps presses, running (pushing off the foot bar), chest expansions, and leg circles were all completed during our testing Pilates workouts to really put these machine to the test.

*Additional reporting by Nicolette Accardi.

#4908. Kraken parent Payward gains market share as slower trading weighs on earnings

Payward’s adjusted EBITDA fell 66% year over year to $60 million, even as its share of global spot trading nearly doubled and fee-based services expanded.

Kraken’s parent company Payward nearly doubled its share of global crypto spot trading to 6.5% in September from 3.3% a year earlier, even as weaker trading activity weighed on its earnings.

The market-share gain means Payward captured a larger portion of spot trading relative to competitors, rather than an increase in trading activity across its platforms. The company handled $353 billion in transactions in the third quarter, down 30% from a year earlier, according to financial results released Friday.

The two figures measure different things. The market share tracks its portion of global spot trading across its platforms in September, compared with a year earlier, while Payward’s quarterly transaction volume includes activity across multiple products, including spot, margin, equities, payments and certain derivatives.

Adjusted EBITDA fell to $60 million from the $178.6 million reported a year earlier. Total platform margin fell 12% to $487 million. Payward introduced that measure this quarter to replace adjusted revenue, adding a deduction for staking rewards paid to customers.

Payward has spent the past two years expanding beyond its core cryptocurrency exchange business through acquisitions in derivatives, proprietary trading, tokenized assets and payments. The strategy aims to diversify revenue beyond transaction fees, which fluctuate with market activity.

Its purchases include futures broker NinjaTrader and proprietary trading firm Breakout in 2025, followed by the acquisition of US-regulated derivatives platform Bitnomial in May 2026. The company also expanded into stablecoin payments with its purchase of Reap in July.

Those businesses contributed to a broader mix of trading and service-based activity in the third quarter. The number of derivatives contracts on which Payward charges a per-contract fee rose 84% to 66 million. Margin from subscriptions, trader evaluations and other paid services rose 59% to $125 million.

Breakout, which charges traders for evaluations that can qualify them for funded trading accounts, was included for the full quarter after joining in September 2025. The July purchase of Reap added a stablecoin payments and card-issuing business. The company did not quantify either acquisition’s contribution to the quarter.

Related: Kraken parent Payward acquires Magic Labs’ wallet business

Results improved from the second quarter despite remaining below year-earlier levels. Total transaction volume rose 22%, while total platform margin increased 12% to $487 million from $436 million.

The improvement was not driven by trading alone. Margin earned from assets customers hold on Payward’s platforms, including staking-related services, rose 26% to $128 million. That accounted for roughly half of the $51 million quarterly increase in total platform margin.

Adjusted EBITDA climbed to $60 million from $23 million, while its margin relative to total platform margin rose to 12% from 5%. Compared with a year earlier, however, adjusted EBITDA was down 66%, underscoring the pressure on profitability despite a growing contribution from services less directly tied to trading activity. Asset- and access-based services accounted for 52% of total platform margin, up from 46% a year earlier.

That shift could matter for an eventual public listing. Payward confidentially filed for a US IPO in November 2025 but paused its plans in March as market conditions weakened. By September, the earliest potential listing window under consideration was the second quarter of 2027.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Improve your game with the latest pickleball-ready shoes.

PICKLEBALL IS A fun way to stay fit, which is especially true if you have the proper gear. This ensures you can make the most of all your matches, which starts from the ground up. Buying a pair of pickleball shoes is one of the smartest investments you can make in your game. Unlike your pickleball paddle, your pickleball shoes have a much more direct relationship to your health. Two of the most important factors to consider are traction and stability.

Like tennis shoes, pickleball shoes need to handle quick movements in all types of directions. That means you want strong outsoles with responsive tread patterns and a midsole structure that can handle fast-twitch lateral movements. Lateral stability is super important since it can help prevent common pickleball injuries to ankles or knees, so it’s more important for them to have a wider base and a stiff lower structure to provide this kind of maximum stability. Our guide to the best pickleball shoes will set you up with the right kind of shoe for enhancing performance while hopefully reducing the odds of rolling an ankle or spraining a knee.

The Rush Pro Ace Pickleball is designed for both indoor and outdoor court surfaces and has a 4D Support Chassis for controlled pivot movements and stability. When we tested it out, The Pickler held tough through all the wear and tear.

The rubber drag pad has helped protect tearing on the end of the toe box, and the cushioned midsole helps keep high foot arches comfortable. The Pickler even has a rebound-like effect when making fast-twitch movements, which makes sense because of how close in construction the shoe is to Pro Ace Tennis Shoe—Wilson's top-selling model for tennis. The rebound of the shoe alone isn't going to make you a better player, but we do believe it helps promote staying on your toes more during play, especially when it comes to getting into a firefight against opponents.

The performance on this shoe is superb, and the style promises a clean look that's suitable for wearing in a country club environment. The comfort of the shoe—namely the supportive arch and cushioned padding around the tongue and ankle—became the final selling point to deem these the best pickleball shoes overall in 2026.

If you’re getting into pickleball for the first time, you don’t want to spend close to $200 just to find out it isn't for you. A great affordable pickleball shoe can help you there—it’s also a great option for those who simply like to budget, too. Enter the second iteration of the Asics Gel-Renma pickleball shoes. A stellar shoe for under $100.

Loaded with similar tech and materials you’ll find in Asics pro-level models, this pair uses a synthetic leather overlay for solid durability as well as its signature Trusstic tech, which helps to enhance stability. To help create a shoe that’s well-balanced for all directional movements, it uses a wrap-up outsole with flex grooves for increased flexibility, and a wider gauge. As Winn notes, "Asics has skyrocketed to the top over the last few years," and this pair is one affordable, high-performance pair.

You might be surprised to find K-Swiss at the top of the pickleball shoe market, but the brand has quietly been creating trusted game-ready models for all types of price points. We've come to find the Express Light as one of the top supportive and strong pickleball shoes money can buy.

Two main features of this shoe stood out when testing: the 180-degree Plantar Support Chassis and the DURAWRAP cover to help combat toe dragging. The support chassis worked great at providing a secure feeling while playing, giving ample support for high arches and preventing feet from twisting and rolling inside the shoe—even when they go hot and sweaty. The DURAWRAP cover is the outsole material used to combat abrasion and toe-dragging. The cover is definitely hard alright, and so it's nice to know you have this strong outer shell over the cushioned mesh that feels oh-so-good on the feet.

The shoes do fit quite snugly, so consider potentially going up a half size on this shoe. The design is unique, and fun with multiple colorways. It's not the fastest shoe, but it provides great durability and support. This is a well-balanced model you can play outside in for long periods of time.

If you’re looking for one lightweight, serious pair of pickleball shoes that can also handle the wear and tear of aggressive game play, the second version of the Viper Courts are definitely the way to go.This go around features a revamped upper that makes them even more durable than the previous gen, while remaining just as breathable and potentially even more comfortable (at least popular opinion says, according to reviewers).

These low tops feature quite the supportive feel with their EVA insoles and responsive foam in the midsoles that are topped off with Goodyear Gold compound soles that can take all the quick cuts and bursts you’ll find yourself doing every game. Plus, they’re versatile enough for the other two big racket sports of tennis and Padel.

New Balance takes the cake when it comes to shoes for those in need of a little extra stability. Both instructors we talked to agree that New Balance always delivers on comfort, support, and above all, stability. Between the precise underfoot cushioning, superior durability, or the FuelCell foam, the elements all come together to form a thoughtful design.

"They're well-made, so they last a long time and are very comfortable," Winn says. Armstrong also adds, "Looking around and asking a few of our senior players, [the New Balances] seem to be a fan favorite." At the end of the day, comfort and stability are the leading factors in selecting a shoe for seniors, both of which this shoe excels in, according to Armstrong.

Babolat doesn't just make stellar tennis racquets; the brand's tennis shoes are in a league of its own. With a soft upper and ventilated mesh, the SFX 4 delivers comfort and breathability in each wear. Babolat doubles down on the comfort with an OrthoLite insole that molds to the shape of your foot. A premium cushioning system absorbs shock in landings, which is super important for comfort and keeping your knees feeling good after a match. The shape and composition of the materials in the sole are segmented into nine key pressure points to deliver maximum responsiveness.

Armstrong also recommends these shoes for beginners. "In my experience, beginners need to look for something that may not require a huge investment, but also provides all the benefits needed to play tennis comfortably and safely," he says. "Generally, the shoes that are in a new player's price range and then feel the best, are the best shoes for them."

Pickleball is a social event and if you want a pair that can go from the courts to drinks afterwards, these Pickle Pro is our choice for sure. With their modern design and streamlined look, you could probably toss on a pair of slacks while wearing these and get away with it. I have worn them out in public running errands multiple times already and have even gotten several compliments on them, they’re that sharp.

Aesthetics aside, these shoes can still hold their own on the courts thanks to their solid design. For starters, these are darn comfortable with their OrthoLite foam midsoles that make them quite plush for a pair of pickleball shoes. Comfy as they are, they are quite tough too, which stems from the Duralast high-density soles that grips well on all court surfaces, but, it does mean they take a bit to break in from my experience. While I wouldn’t necessarily choose them for ultra competitive games, for a stylish and casual game, these are an absolute winner.

The Barricade is a go-to for all training sessions and matches for players who prioritize comfort. When shopping for shoes, Armstrong says, "Players have different criteria as to what makes a shoe great. Personally, I want something that is durable, supportive but not too bulky, and comfortable." Armstrong, who teaches/plays almost every day of the week, needs something that feels good on his notoriously aching Achilles tendon. Adidas makes this pair that does all of this, and are even a favorite of Armstrong's father (who tore his Achilles a few years ago) because of their unrivaled comfort.

Wonder why? It might have something to do with the shoe's foam Geofit Sensepods to securely lock in the heel, a cushioned Bounce midsole, and asymmetrical laces to help guard against the effects of foot drag. There's also a sustainability component, with 50 percent of the yarn in the upper being recycled.

If your the type of player who loves to chase down every shot, you’re going to need a shoe that can keep up. That means you’re going to want a pair that flexes and moves with your natural foot strike, allowing you to stay light on the balls of your feet. One of the best in the game right now that allows just those types of movement patterns are the CourtStrike Pro 2.0s from Selkirk.

Thanks to their 3D printing, you get a secure shoe with excellent lateral stability and a super responsive EVA midsole that helps to drastically improve you're reaction time. This allows you to stay explosive and react at will.

This 2.0 model features better, more durable rubber, extra material protection along the bottom of the laces for increased longevity, and multiple layered cushioning for a springier step. If you’re on a budget, you may want to opt for another pair on our list, but if you want one of the most versatile pairs around, just get these.

Pickleball shoes need to provide support, so buying the lightest shoe possible is not the smartest move. When buying a lightweight shoe (say, under 10 ounces) there's likely to be some sacrifice in support or stability. The trick? Stick to pickleball-specific shoes first. You can also consider tennis shoes and cross-trainers due to their similar support-first construction. Avoid featherlight running shoes that are built for a different type of movement.

Mesh is the most common and best material to look for in the upper of a pickleball shoe. However, like weight, you don't necessarily need the most breathable mesh possible. Some pickleball shoes sacrifice breathability to boost abrasion resistance, and to help keep your foot secure (like limiting your foot rolling and turning inside the shoe).

When it comes to the outsole, look for a shoe that has a strong rubber pattern that will help grip surfaces and reduce the odds of slipping when turning your feet. Some pickleball shoes pay greater attention to tread pattern, which can help provide a feeling of better grip on a court. Outsole will largely come down to personal preference, as most are constructed about the same.

When looking at the midsole, aim for a shoe that has supportive cushioning (like EVA foam) and keeps a relatively low profile. Prioritizing a midsole with too much cushioning could lead you to a shoe that sits high (like a Hoka running shoe), thus leading to a less responsive design, which could potentially lead to a greater chance of rolling an ankle when making fast turns on the court.

I have been fortunate enough to rock quite a few pairs of pickleball shoes over the past few years. Having played on multiple surfaces, I’ve learned a few things about what to look for when selecting a pair. I also partnered with our other writers and editors at Men's Health to help select the best pickleball shoes we’ve tested in the past few years, available. We’ve compiled a guide to the best all-day play, taking great note of each shoe's stability, durability, weight, and price point. Special consideration was taken into account for pickleball shoes that had excellent traction and stability since those two qualities are the most important in a pickleball shoe.

There is a lot of crossover from effective tennis shoes to pickleball shoes. So we also spoke to experts like Life Time Galleria Tennis Leader Gary Armstrong (who has been playing tennis for 36 years and has been an instructor for 17 years) and Life Time Charlotte Tennis Leader Eric Winn (who has been a tennis coach for 24 years and still plays in the 5.0 USTA leagues) to get their takes on the best tennis shoes for men. With minimal differences, some of their picks made it to this guide.

If you're someone who's going to play pickleball once or twice for recreation, then you could get away with a low-profile running shoe. But if you're expecting to play any more than that, we strongly recommend buying a proper pair of pickleball shoes.

The reason we don't recommend wearing just any type of running shoe is that running shoes are made for forward motion, so there's often less emphasis on reinforcing the shoe for side-to-side movements. Running shoes also have less structure and stability than what you want in a pickleball shoe, as the running styles these days are made to be as lightweight and breathable as possible (with high cushioned stacks), which means less focus on overall support.

So, to be clear, you should steer from wearing running shoes for pickleball if you expect to play the game on a regular basis. A proper pickleball shoe is a smart investment that will help give you traction and stability while greatly decreasing the chance of rolling an ankle or spraining a knee.

#4904. Adam Back makes case for simpler security as Blockstream launches Bitcoin custody system

Blockstream’s new custody system, developed with Thales, uses dedicated hardware for transaction signing as Adam Back advocates for offline security to reduce cyber risks.

Adam Back’s Bitcoin infrastructure company Blockstream has launched a new institutional digital asset custody solution developed with French technology group Thales, as the cryptographer pushes for simpler, offline security systems to protect Bitcoin against increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.

The solution, announced Friday, combines Thales’ hardware security modules (HSMs) with Blockstream’s Secure Multi-Party Computation (Secure-MPC) technology, allowing institutions to authorize transactions while keeping sensitive cryptographic operations within dedicated security hardware, according to the company.

Unlike conventional MPC implementations that may perform portions of the signing process outside dedicated security hardware, Blockstream said its architecture executes the entire signing protocol within the protected environment of Thales’ HSMs.

Blockstream co-founder and CEO Adam Back, a pioneering cryptographer whose Hashcash system helped lay the groundwork for Bitcoin’s proof-of-work mechanism, told Cointelegraph that conventional MPC protocols are often too complex and require too much communication between devices to be practical for fully offline cold storage.

“When people talk about MPC, they’re talking about some very esoteric and complicated protocols that are hard to secure and are very interactive. So you can’t really use them in a cold storage setting,” Back said.

Related: Blockstream rejects ransom as Liquid hackers hold nearly 600 BTC

Back pointed to the Binance $6.3 billion hack as an example of the risks facing internet-connected custody infrastructure, arguing that keeping signing devices offline can help prevent unauthorized access.

According to Binance’s investigation, attackers compromised employee devices and obtained credentials that allowed them to access the exchange’s wallet-signing infrastructure.

He also said that AI could make existing security challenges more difficult to manage, particularly by helping attackers discover subtle flaws in complex MPC implementations.

“The AIs can help attackers find small implementation errors and things like that, which may not be obvious,” he said.

Asked whether the broader custody industry would adopt similar offline security models, Back said he hoped so, arguing that institutions should “adapt to the environment” by moving assets into cold storage to reduce exposure to potential AI-assisted attacks.

“Complexity is the enemy of security. And going back to basics is the answer, you know, just cold-store it,” Back added.

For starters, most laser hair removal devices have about 200,000 flashes or the equivalent of 780 at-home treatments, Dr. Nazarian previously told us in our guide to the best facial hair removal devices. This IPL device has double that, aka 1,560 treatments, meaning the investment will last for several years even with consistent use. Each hair removal sesh will only cost you $0.31, which is a third of the price of a Wet n Wild eyeliner.

Next, it’s our only recommended device that connects to a compatible smartphone app via Bluetooth and Wi-Fi technology to tailor your treatment to your needs. Wohlner was impressed with how well the intuitive app assessed her skin tone and hair color for compatibility.

Wohlner admits that she never used interchangeable heads before because they were intimidating. However, Braun solved that problem because the app told her what head to use for different parts of her body. The software even analyzes how much coverage Wohlner needs to ensure she doesn't miss any spots. Lastly, the app has a built-in calendar, so she’ll always remember when she’s due for some zaps—something Wohlner admits can be hard to keep track of, but is key for results.

Like other Braun laser hair removal devices we've tried, this one comes in a sturdy carrying case that keeps everything neatly organized under your vanity, or wherever you choose to store it. The unit doesn't call out any specific cooling technology, but Wohlner said her experience was largely pain-free. "I felt a little zippiness here and there, but nothing I could actually describe as painful—more like a super quick, tiny pinch," she says.

As for the results, they were solid. Wohlner typically shaves her self-described super coarse hair daily until she started using this device. She was impressed that she didn’t need to shave her underarms for weeks after her first treatment. "After three more sessions, I saw a pretty major payoff,” says Wohlner. “There are definitely a few hairs still popping through, but they've grown back so slowly."

Overall, this device is pricey, but for someone serious about tackling the hair on their body—whether armpits, legs, Brazilian area, and beyond—it's worth every penny, especially if you feel like you could use a little help through the process.

Truly the only thing we don’t enjoy about this device is the price tag. However, it has 400,000 flashes—double the average of our other favorite devices—which means this Braun can easily last you 30 years. Genius!

If you can't stomach the price of Braun's latest and greatest IPL, the brand’s cheaper Silk Expert Pro 5 is hardly a downgrade. In our comprehensive test, Earley found the device to be both easy to use and highly effective.

The Silk Expert Pro 5 removes all of Earley’s unwanted hair after just four weeks of use. "I was so happy to say goodbye to my leg and armpit hair,” says the working mom of four. “Anything that saves me time—and trust me, not having to shave is a huge time-saver—is something I'm 100% willing to invest in." The ergonomic handle is easier to hold than the bulky, cheaper alternatives that remind her of hair dryers. For larger areas of her body, Earley holds down the trigger for continuous flashes—a feature she says speeds things up immensely.

Compared to our best overall pick, the Silk Expert Pro 5 lacks convenience features like a compatible smartphone app that allows you to tailor your treatments and track coverage areas to make sure you don't miss any spots. It does, however, have a proprietary SensoAdapt technology, which uses a built-in sensor to continuously and automatically read your skin tone and self-adjust the energy setting for safety and efficacy just like its more expensive counterpart.

Overall, it's a worthy pick—as evidenced by Earley’s testing experience and its popularity on Amazon and TikTok—if you're looking to spend a little bit less and don't mind sacrificing a few features.

We’ve been testing and liking Ulike devices since 2022. From the ULike Sapphire Air+ to the Air 3, and now the featured Air 10 is the brand’s latest model worth owning.

Instead of buying two devices, the Air 10 works quite literally from your face to your toes. The latest version is equipped with dual lights to zap hair on your upper lip, bikini area, underarms, and legs. It offers four modes, including a new setting for stubborn hairs. The gentle intensity setting zaps hair from the face, while the strongest mode uses high-speed flashes to speed up removing unwanted face and body hair.

What we like most is that Air 10 is easy to use and relatively pain-free. While other devices use heat to remove hair, the Ulike Air 10 cools itself down to 65 degrees Fahrenheit. This chilly surface helps lower your skin temperature to prevent irritation and burns from overheating. Maberry says the cooling tech found in both the Air 3 and Air 10 models is especially useful for sensitive areas like the bikini line.

It’s also a relatively low time commitment of 20 to 30 minutes for a full treatment while watching TV. "Once you get the hang of how to use the device, it's super easy to zap, zap, zap while you scroll through TikTok,” Maberry said in her review. Ulike promises visible results within four weeks, but Maberry saw her hair thin in just three weeks. The hair-free appearance was so dramatic around week six that Maberry was tempted to stop the treatments entirely. She continued using it for the recommended 12 weeks and now hairs only pop up every four to six weeks.

One thing to note: the built-in cooling fan is a bit noisy, so Maberry turns up her TV volume slightly. Still, the tradeoff isn’t a real dealbreaker: "I would rather have a painless device that makes little noise than a silent one that causes a burning sensation," she said. It’s also worth mentioning that this device is best suited for someone with fair to olive complexions and brown to black hair. The tech can’t accurately differentiate between a deeper skin tone and dark tresses.

This budget-conscious device seems a little too good to be true, but it earned a casual 4-star average from nearly 12,900 Amazon reviews. More than 7,330 of these reviews are a perfect 5-star rating. Not too shabby! Shoppers rave about using this IPL device on their face and body, including the ultra-sensitive bikini line.

Like other laser hair removal devices, this IPL tool features a manual mode that emits a single flash at a time to precisely target areas, like the chin, upper lip, and armpits. There is also an auto mode that emits continuous flashes for the legs, stomach, and arms. And FWIW, this device comes with an epic 36-month warranty and 100-day money-back policy, which is more than triple the regular return window of other Amazon beauty products.

The main complaint about this price-friendly tool is that it’s bulky, making it less ideal for travel. However, it does boast an ergonomic design for an overall comfortable hair removal experience. And since each treatment area requires a maximum of two minutes or less, you won’t have to worry about any discomfort for your wrist.

If you’re like us, then you’re probably a bit surprised that an at-home laser hair removal device can be so costly. However, we put this one to the test for nearly two months and saw major results. Based on our long-term testing experience, Epilaser’s effective tech, and the sophisticated design and feel, we knew it was deserving of a spot on this list. We adored it so much that we featured it as one of the best beauty launches of 2025 in our annual Skincare Awards package.

Our deputy visual director, Dangi McCoy, usesd this laser two to three times a week for two months on her right underarm to compare the results. She noticed the treated area regrew hair more slowly, and had half the amount of underarm hair compared to her left side. “At seven weeks, I’m still using the laser, but the regrowth has been so sparse I could count the hairs at a glance,” McCoy said in her Epilaser review.

Notably, this is the only featured device that use diode lasers for hair removal. As a quick reminder, using the wrong laser type, aka IPL, can cause burns in dark brown and deep skin tones. Thankfully, the Epilaser’s diodes prevent this from happening. The device’s unique laser wavelength bypasses the melanin that gives our skin its pigment, allowing it to safely remove hair rather than mistaking our skin for dark hair.

Epilaser is also extremely functional when you have limited outlets in your home or hotel room. During McCoy’s testing process, she found some of the cords to be cumbersome, so it was nice to have the flexibility of charging her device and using it cordless. It also allowed McCoy to remove hair from anywhere in her home, such as the couch while watching Uptown Girls.

OK, so what about the discomfort? Is splurging really worth it in this case? Turns out, yes! Epilaser maximizes hair removal results even if you have a low tolerance for discomfort. While no laser hair removal device is completely painless, McCoy only felt occasional quick pricks on her skin. The brand’s proprietary SPOT technology zaps up to 15 hairs per second, while leaving your skin untouched.

She was also impressed by how lightweight the cordless Epilaser felt in her hands. The device feels sturdy, and its ergonomic design enhances comfort during longer treatment sessions. Plus, this laser hair removal device looks absolutely gorgeous IRL—the bronze-tone trim truly elevates the luxurious appearance.

Given the laser’s smaller opening, you can even use this device on your face. It also comes with a soft-sided travel case with a short handle strap that’s easy to pack in your carry-on or rolling suitcase.

SmoothSkin's system works for anyone who wants something that's easy to use and doesn't require a lot of manual work or tinkering with buttons or various features. A patented sensor measures your skin before each flash and automatically selects the light best suited to your skin tone. This helps speed up the whole process, so full-body treatments take approximately 10 minutes.

It also includes a precision head to target smaller areas of the body—like the bikini line or even the upper lip or chin. The adaptable head also makes it easier to follow along your natural curves, like your kneecaps or underarms.

Like other great laser hair removal devices on the market, this one promises visible hair reduction in as little as four weeks and complete results by 12 weeks. It works so well that you’ll notice a difference after just one use, which is a true testament to this laser's power. SmoothSkin is on the pricey side, but justified by the fact that it offers unlimited flashes, allowing you to use this device for life. Overall, an excellent value over its lengthy lifetime. No wonder it earned 250 five-star Amazon reviews.

You've probably seen this popular laser hair removal device on your social media feeds, and our team says it really does live up to the hype. Nood’s proprietary PrecisionPulse laser makes all of the difference. The IPL flashes every 10 milliseconds, meaning it exposes your skin to less light that could accidentally cause burns.

Nood’s combination of continuous flashes and larger window make it better suited for larger areas, especially the legs. You can polish them off in 15 to 20 minutes, though it's harder to target smaller areas, like the upper lip. We also love the large digital display on this model.

It makes it very easy to toggle through the seven different intensity levels, and it's always clear which one you're working on. The price is friendlier than some other options, plus the brand offers a 90-day money-back guarantee, which makes this device a great option for anyone on the fence about at-home laser hair removal.

There are a lot of laser hair removal devices on the market, which is why you should consider a few of these pointers before investing.

IPL and diode lasers both slow hair growth and reduce the thickness of individual strands by scanning for pigment and targeting the hair follicle, says dermatologist Melanie Kingsley, MD. But, they each have their benefits and limitations.

IPL is the most commonly used type of light in at-home laser hair removal devices. This technology uses broad-spectrum light to target melanin, the pigment that gives your hair its color. The light is also unsuitable for dark and deep skin tones because it can’t distinguish between melanin-rich skin and the pigment of dark hair, says dermatologist Rachel Nazarian, MD. However, if you have a fair to olive complexion with dark hair, then you’re an ideal candidate for IPL treatments.

Until recently, all at-home laser hair removal devices were IPL lasers. But Epilaser has a game-changing laser for home use. Unlike IPL lights, which emit a broad spectrum of light ranging from 400 to 1,400 nm, diode lasers are unique because they use a more concentrated wavelength of light (around 810 nm). This precise wavelength means it can better target the hair follicles rather than accidentally burning your skin, making it more accessible for some people with darker complexions.

Both are effective, but diode lasers are slightly more versatile. That said, no matter which one you go with, you’ll need multiple treatments to maintain your hair-free results.

One of the biggest considerations is the number of flashes a device is equipped to deliver. This number indicates how long the device will last, according to Dr. Nazarian. "Many devices contain about 200,000 flashes, which is typically good for more than 15 years, although it also depends on how many areas you’re treating," she says. Other recommendations on this list, like the Smoothskin, have unlimited flashes, which means they'll theoretically last forever, but are pricier.

Extra features like multiple intensity modes—lower options for sensitive skin; higher settings for those who want to see results fast (see the Nood)—or interchangeable heads for precise treatment all over the body (hi, Braun) can increase the price. The amount you spend comes down to the features you want in your device and how long you want it to last.

One of the best ways to reduce discomfort during laser hair removal is to use cooling technology. It lowers your skin’s temperature—before, during, and after each laser pulse—to help you better tolerate longer and higher treatment settings safely.

Devices with bigger heads are more efficient on large areas. For more targeted flashes, opt for rigs with compact heads, such as the Iouniya Laser Hair Removal, which can be used on both the face and body. If you have sensitive skin, consider stretching your treatments out to once a month to start and gradually up the frequency once your skin can handle the laser hair removal treatment. The final hair-free results will take longer to achieve but at least you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, she says you’ll notice thinning hair after your first four treatments.

Once you choose your device, know that it can take some time to see results. While every device is different, you’ll probably use it weekly anywhere from four to 10 weeks before noticing lasting results, says dermatologist Bertha Baum, DO. The final results might take longer to achieve, but you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, warm weather likely won’t return until April or early May, meaning you’ve got several weeks to achieve smooth results. Either way, Dr. Baum says you’ll notice thinning hair after your first four treatments.

This technology has come a long way and, while pricey, it's a long-term investment that pays for itself. Think of it this way: A laser that costs $500 is basically the same price as a professional hair removal session, and that in-office treatment won't last forever, but you will continue using your at-home laser for years. And FWIW, we found a few discounted, top-rated Amazon picks that start at just $42, but you’ll want to hurry since these are fleeting deals.

At Women’s Health, we prioritize hands-on editor testing to ensure you don’t waste your time or money. Ahead is insight on what went into our editorial process while trying the latest and greatest at-home laser hair removal devices.

After testing these devices since February 2022, beauty director Brian Underwood, deputy deals and trends editor Eunice Lucero-Lee, and luxury commerce editor Sarah Maberry whittled down this list to 12 of the best laser hair removal devices. We also tapped contributors Jasmine Gomez, Lily Wohlner, and Brigitt Earley to ensure these devices work across most skin tones.

They all boast impressive features, are comfortable to use, and offer incredible value. Plus, these picks are FDA-cleared, so they’ve been evaluated for safety and efficacy. Several dermatologists also shared their no-fail laser hair removal tips and best-in-class product recommendations.

And because we know what it’s like to ball on a budget, we also considered pricing. TBH, laser hair removal devices aren’t exactly cheap. Many cost between $300 and $600, especially when shopping for these expert-approved devices from well-respected brands, such as Braun.

To help, I carefully researched dozens of other cheaper, yet top-rated Amazon laser hair removal devices. Ultimately, I found four Amazon picks that are aligned with expert guidance and are currently discounted as low as $35. Talk about major savings! For added peace of mind, they all earned thousands of rave reviews from real Amazon customers.

So if you're ready to ditch daily shaving and bi-monthly waxing, we're confident—based on our own testing and our dermatologists' advice—that this list contains only the best, most effective options on the market worth your hard-earned coins.

Dr. Nazarian confirms at-home laser hair removal devices are generally safe and effective, citing a 2019 paper. The biggest challenge with many at-home devices comes down to their inability to differentiate between dark skin and dark hair due to their pigmentation. Melanin-rich complexions risk absorbing too much laser energy that increases the risk for burning, cautions Dr. Nazarian. If this is you, then see your dermatologist for a recommendation on the best laser hair removal treatments and devices.

It's also a good idea to do a patch test and not expose the treated area to sunlight for a week, says Dr. Shirazi. Your treated skin is temporarily more sensitive, and you risk sunburn, hyperpigmentation, and delayed healing. She also doesn’t suggest using the laser on tanned and tattooed skin, open wounds, moles, or birthmarks to avoid changing their appearance or causing accidental burns.

Truthfully, they're not optimal for sensitive or dark skin. Many at-home devices cannot distinguish between melanin-rich complexions and dark hair, says dermatologist Corey L. Hartman, MD. Anyone else can still give them a try.

And, like with salon treatments, it's important to practice patience—this isn't a "one and done" situation. Many devices need to be used multiple times weekly to achieve the initial results. Plus, each at-home session can take 10 to 60 minutes, depending on how much body and facial hair you plan to remove. While a tad annoying upfront, this minor inconvenience has a major payoff because your hair will regrow slower over time with regular use.

#4901. The 7 Best Head Shavers for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Get the chrome dome of your dreams with these scalp shavers.

AS MEN, THE decision to go bald isn’t always one that’s made for us (thanks, genetics). But how you deal with hair loss is entirely in your hands. Sure, there are some viable hair loss treatments and shampoos for thinning hair that we certainly back. For many men, it's easier to just bite the bullet and shave their hair completely to offset any future thinning woes. If you are one of these men, more power to you! Hell, some men do it even if they’re not experiencing hair loss—and that’s cool, too. Investing in a quality head shaver will double down on the convenience factor of being bald by making the entire process seamless.

When you do choose to shave your head, the tools you use to do it are paramount. That’s where the best head shavers come in. These high-tech gadgets are specifically designed to make shaving your head easier, whether it’s through a multi-head ergonomic design or close-cutting technology (or both).

Far easier than heading to the barbershop every few days, these electric shavers are meant to be used at home. Think of them as an easier, safer, and quicker alternative to carefully taking a razor to your dome. But before investing in a shaver, there are a few key factors to keep in mind to ensure you select the absolute best one for you.

This tiny but powerful shaver is designed to give your scalp the closest shave possible, whether you prefer to do it dry, wet, or with the aid of other products. The five ScalpSafe shaving heads wrap around the curves of your head for a microscopically close shave, and the additional attachments, like a pre-shave exfoliation brush and precision trimmer, are nice bonuses.

Our editors also love that it pairs nicely with our favorite shaving creams and pre-shave oils, in case you want an even deeper cut. Its portable design makes it easy to carry in your luggage, though its travel case is sold separately. Not to mention, the five heads of this shaver definitely give an incredibly close shave—as close as the Remington and the Braun, both of which we found to be top of the heap in our testing process.

We also appreciate the additional attachments that this one comes with, unlike the Remington, particularly the pre-shave exfoliating brush, which not only helps give a closer shave, but also feels pretty damn good on your dome (you’ll want to only use this if you have a tiny bit of stubble though—the bristles aren’t long enough to reach through longer hair).

In theory, the trimmer attachment and the accompanying guards are great if you want to trim your beard (the brand also says you can use it to trim your body and other areas), but we found that the design of the device makes that difficult. Since it’s meant to be held in the palm of your hand, it’s not as easy to use on your face as a more traditional razor design like the Braun or even the Andis. We would probably skip that and relegate this device to only our heads, which, at a comparable price point to other models like the Remington, is OK.

Read More: How to Give Yourself a Buzzcut

If you’re in a rush, this easy-to-use shaver may be your answer. Thanks to the pivoting shaver heads that hug each curve of your head, the brand says that this device can shave your entire head in just two minutes.

After testing the Remington Balder Pro for over a year, we can safely say that it easily gave us a head shave in less than five minutes, which is great for guys who cut their dome weekly. We love the hair capture chamber, which collects hair for easy cleanup, and its non-slip grip gives you extra control when you're mowing through your head.

Keep in mind that this is designed only for head shaving, so if you’re looking for a more multi-purpose solution, you’ll want to go with a more traditional electric shaver like the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus. And since there aren’t any additional attachments like the kind that come with others, like the Freebird, you’re really only going to use this to give your head a smooth, clean shave (which it is frankly very good at doing).

The price is comparable to other head shavers, but we found that the performance outmatches them, so it’s a great investment if you’re a guy who shaves his head often and doesn’t mind having a separate tool just for that task.

If you’re not the smooth-shave type, but still want to give yourself a close buzz without heading to the barber, the Shortcut Pro delivers. With multiple length options via interchangeable combs, this shaver allows you to try different buzz looks on your own.

As the product image suggests, the Shortcut Pro is super compact, which makes it great for tossing in a Dopp kit and taking on trips. The feel of the shaver takes a second to get used to, but once you learn how to wield it, you'll find it does a solid job of staying cut-free while providing a solid shave.

It’s worth repeating that this won’t give you a close, clean shave, but it is handy if you like more of a stubble look. The design isn’t perfect and is less ergonomic than the Remington or one of the similarly designed shavers, but once you get the hang of it, it’s pretty foolproof.

Our one gripe is that because of the curved design, which is nice for hugging the shape of your head, it’s a bit difficult for detailed work around your ears or cleaning up your neck. A more traditional clipper is better for those things, but that’s a small price to pay for the convenience this one offers.

Like Braun’s previous versions, the Series 9 Pro+ has proven to be effective in performance. Not only is it one of our favorite head shavers, but it’s seen as the “Rolls-Royce of shaving instruments” by Faheem Alexander, barber and owner of Faheem's Hands of Precision in Philadelphia.“I highly recommend [it] because of the unparalleled ease and comfort it provides while also ensuring a super close shave,” he says. “The accompanying portable charging case makes this super easy to throw in a bag and get numerous weeks of shaves without plugging it in.”

During our trial run, we found out that the fast-speed device can cut up to 40,000 cuts per minute. Thanks to its waterproof capability, you can use it in the shower for a refreshing shaving experience. We also love that the device comes with a SmartCare center, which maintains the quality for longer use and makes cleaning up a breeze.

While this isn’t technically a head shaver in the way the two Remingtons or Freebird are, we found in our testing that it performs just as well at shaving your head as it does at shaving your face—it is our best electric razor.

What that means to us is that if you’re looking to streamline the number of devices you have in your arsenal, but don’t want to sacrifice power or efficacy, this is an ideal option. It’s expensive—as the Rolls-Royce of shaving instruments is expected to be—but if you’re using it for multiple things like shaving your head and face, that helps justify the cost a bit more.

Ever wonder how your barber gets such a close shave when he’s doing skin fades or cleaning up your neck? Enter this foil shaver, which is hard to beat when it comes to closeness. Not to mention, it’s a go-to for plenty of barbers. Speaking of which, Alexander gives the Andis tool his stamp of approval because it works efficiently for shaving experiences at home and in the barbershop.

It operates well on battery, delivering up to 80 minutes of run time on a single charge—a duration that’s twice as long as others on this list. The price point may be higher than most on this list, but the results make up for the difference.

This is definitely a classic for a reason—it really gets the job done with an incredibly smooth shave. However, it’s aggressive and not the gentlest experience, especially if you’re just beginning with it. Theoretically, you can use this on your face and other areas, too, but we found that the shaving experience is too harsh for us to use anywhere but our head and neck. You’ll also likely want to finish with some sort of lotion or moisturizer to minimize potential irritation.

Manscaped is one of the most consistent brands in men’s grooming, and this head shaver is a perfect example of why. It simply gets the basics right for a more enjoyable, less irritating shave. The grip, which invites palming, is super user-friendly, making moving the blades along your head easy with minimal effort (or risk of dropping it).

The brand’s signature SkinSafe blade guards make cuts and nicks rare, while the magnetic connection makes clean-up and replacements easy. With a 9,500 RPM motor, it shaves smoothly and efficiently. We found it also required minimal passes to get a full shave. Adding to its user-friendliness, the Dome Shaver Pro battery lasts up to 90 minutes and is USB-C chargeable. Plus, it’s waterproof and includes a sturdy hard-shell travel case.

This head shaver from the always reliable Philips Norelco is a great choice if you’re looking for a smooth, comfortable shave without the hassle. Its 360-degree flexing head follows the contours of your scalp, while the 36 self-sharpening ComfortCut blades deliver an even shave without putting unnecessary pressure on your skin.

The ergonomic grip makes it easy to maneuver, while the PowerAdapt Sensor automatically adjusts power to match hair density as you go. With up to 90 minutes of cordless use, water resistance, and a convenient travel case, it’s a reliable option for both everyday grooming and travel.

Most head shavers feature multiple razor heads to help hug the contours of your head so you can easily navigate areas that are hard to see. The multiple razor heads can also help limit cuts, as the design adjusts to curved angles much better than a single, straight razor.

For the quickest, most adaptable (read: lowest maintenance) shaving experience, look for devices with shaving heads in the five-to-seven range, like the Freebird FlexSeries or Remington Balder Pro. That being said, don’t fall into the common trap of thinking that more shaving heads automatically equals a more powerful shave, as the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus is one of the most powerful options on the market and only has four shaving blades.

Most head shavers on this list can be used dry, which means as long as your hair is already short enough (no more than a couple of days of growth), you can shave with no moisture or product. What's also great is that some options are waterproof, making your shaving experience in the shower a total breeze and easy to clean up.

Plus, you can use most wet/dry shavers with shaving products, so if you prefer to begin with a pre-shave oil to protect your scalp and then add a shaving cream or lotion to help with gliding. Follow it up by rinsing the product off your head—just make sure to also clean any leftover product from the razor heads before you put it away. However, there are a couple of options we recommend that do not have this capability, so if you’re a dedicated shower shaver, focus solely on the wet/dry devices.

A good cordless head shaver can last as long as 90 minutes, which means you can go a whole week without charging the battery. They also unlock the ability to shave in the shower or on the road without having to be plugged in. If you're constantly on the move and shave your head regularly, you will find that cordless options offer lots of convenience and save even more time.

Even before joining the bald brotherhood, most of us have all had an electric razor or beard trimmer die out before we've finished the job. Nobody wants to sport a half-trimmed beard or uneven body hair, but the absolute last spot you'll want an uneven shave is on your dome, as it's the hardest to hide.

To avoid walking around with a patchy skull, keep battery life in mind when choosing an electric shaver. Consider how long you typically take to shave your entire head—and how often you tend to charge devices—before finalizing your decision.

The first question to ask is: Does this shaver come with a case included? If yes, then you're going to want to look at what type of case it is. For frequent travelers, a carrying case made to fit neatly in a Dopp kit or luggage should be a priority. However, if you're just looking for something to store it in, you can allow for more size, given that it'll more easily hold every attachment or replacement piece, so there won't be any long search involved when needed.

#4900. OpenAI launches AI payments in ChatGPT with Visa, Mastercard and Amex

OpenAI’s new payment wallet lets AI agents complete purchases using existing card networks, with plans to eventually allow preauthorized transactions.

OpenAI on Friday introduced a new feature allowing AI agents to make purchases on behalf of users directly within ChatGPT through existing payment networks, in collaboration with American Express, Mastercard and Visa.

The wallet lets users authorize transactions using biometric verification, such as facial recognition or fingerprints. Payment networks generate tokenized card credentials for each approved purchase, keeping users’ actual card details from merchants and AI agents, the company said.

The launch comes as AI companies seek to move beyond product recommendations into executing transactions, potentially changing how consumers interact with online merchants. OpenAI said it is working with payment processors and fraud prevention firms to support AI purchases through existing checkout systems.

OpenAI joins a growing field of companies developing payment systems for AI agents. Google introduced its Agent Payments Protocol in 2025, while Visa and Mastercard have launched initiatives to support AI-initiated transactions.

Crypto companies are also developing payment infrastructure for AI agents. Coinbase introduced its x402 protocol in 2025, enabling autonomous stablecoin payments for digital services, while Circle launched its Agent Stack in May, allowing agents to hold and spend USDC within predefined limits. Crossmint, which provides stablecoin infrastructure, has taken a different approach, combining stablecoin wallets with traditional card networks.

Global agentic commerce transaction value is expected to reach $1.5 trillion by 2030, according to an April report from Juniper Research, up from an estimated $8 billion in 2026.
