#4834. Toyota’s Corolla Cross EV spotted for the first time [Images]

Toyota is giving its best-selling Corolla a major makeover, and an all-electric version is part of the plan. The upcoming Corolla Cross EV was captured in public for the first time ahead of its expected 2027 debut.

The Corolla has always been “a car for everyone,” Toyota’s former president and current CEO, Koji Sato, said after unveiling the next-gen Corolla Concept at last year’s Japan Mobility Show.

Since it went on sale 60 years ago, over 57 million drivers have chosen the Corolla, making it Toyota’s best-selling vehicle ever.

The Corolla has undergone 12 model changes since 1966, but the compact car is about to undergo its biggest transformation yet.

Although it’s still a top seller, the Corolla has lost some of its appeal as new, more advanced, and efficient options have emerged. Toyota looks to change that with the next-generation model.

It will remain “a car for everyone,” as Sato said, but the next-gen Corolla will come in multiple powertrains, including an all-electric version.

“Whether it’s a battery EV, plug-in hybrid, hybrid, or internal combustion engine vehicle―whatever the power source―let’s make good-looking cars that everyone will want to drive,” Sato said at the Japan Mobility Show last October.

Ahead of its expected debut sometime in 2027, a disguised Corolla Cross EV was spotted driving near Toyota’s European headquarters and R&D center.

New images from Chinese media outlet Autohome show what’s expected to be the all-electric Corolla Cross, with a closed-off grille and a unique body design.

The new Corolla will be the first to use Toyota’s new “multipathway” platform that will support electric, hybrid, gas, and other powertrains.

Toyota hasn’t revealed specifics, including battery or powertrain specs, but the next-gen Corolla EV is expected to remain close in style to the Concept. Aside from the massive COROLLA badge on the back, it looks like an entirely different vehicle with a near sports-car-like silhouette.

In an exclusive interview with Japanese media NHK in July, Toyota’s current chairman and former CEO, Akio Toyoda, warned that the company “cannot survive” if it does not adapt amid new competition and technology from China.

During the special, which went behind the scenes at Toyota’s “top secret” development site, several blurred Corolla Concept body types, including a sedan, hatchback, crossover, and GR model, were revealed in the background.

According to a recent Nikkei report, Toyota plans to begin production of the next-gen Corolla in 2028 through its joint venture with Chinese state-owned FAW Group, FAW Toyota Motor.

The Toyota Corolla EV is expected to be available in single- and dual-motor configurations with a driving range of at least 250 miles.

Let's hope that Toyota gets the Corolla EV right, because if it offers the right range for the right price but still feels fundamentally like a Corolla it is an EV that would get consideration from buyers who wouldn't otherwise consider an EV.

They're the buyers that trust Toyota and who consider the Corolla to be a nice safe choice for a car. And by safe, that means a vehicle that may not be all that exciting, but also a vehicle that they won't regret buying. Needless to say, these are not people who read Electrek, or even Car & Driver, for that matter. But there's a lot more of them than there are of us.

The hybrid version will reportedly use a new 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine and an electric motor. Toyota’s engineers told Car and Driver the system would deliver around 134 horsepower. It’s also estimated to be 10% to 20% more efficient than the current Corolla.

Toyota has yet to confirm the electric version will launch in the US. According to Car and Driver, the gas version will likely start at around $25,000, the hybrid around $27,000, and the EV and PHEVs will likely be priced in the $30,000 range.

#4833. Could Your GLP-1s Make You Blind? Here’s What to Make of the FDA’s Latest Notice.

For years, there have been rumblings and even research about a rare but serious condition that’s been linked to taking a GLP-1 medication. Now, the Food and Drug Administration is doing something about it.

The FDA just released a drug safety communication to warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential increased risk of developing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) when you take a GLP-1 medication. NAION is a rare condition that can lead to vision loss in one eye, and it can be permanent.

Again, this isn't the first time concerns have been raised about the risk of NAION. But it is the first time the FDA has issued a warning about it.

Given that up to 11 percent of Americans currently take a GLP-1 for weight loss, this news stands to impact a lot of people. How concerned should you be if you're one of them? Eye experts and a doctor who prescribes GLP-1s break it down.

Meet the experts: Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system; Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute; and Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

The FDA's notice is designed to flag the potential risk of NAION to people who use GLP-1s. The FDA also notes that the agency will require all manufacturers of GLP-1 medications to add information about the risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section of their labels.

"Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss, with GLP-1 RA use," the notice reads.

The agency cited a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology as well as its own meta-analyses and retrospective cohort study in the notice. They also noted that “NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products.”

However, the complication remains rare: incidents from the FDA’s meta-analysis were just 6.4 events per 100,000 per year for patients using the medications.

The warning is just that—a warning to patients and physicians that this could happen, explains Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. "Most outcome-related issues in medicine should be thought of as being probabilistic—there is a certain chance that events can occur," he says. "This warning indicates that the FDA has reason to believe, at least at this time, that the probability of NAION occurring is higher in patients who take GLP-1 RA drugs."

But Dr. Rizzo stresses that there's no evidence that these drugs cause NAION—just that there's a link.

So…why issue a warning if it's not proven that GLP-1s cause NAION and it's so rare? "The severity of a complication matters alongside its frequency," says Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute. "Even a rare risk deserves attention when it can permanently affect vision." The warning is likely designed to give healthcare providers a heads-up that it could be NAION if a patient has symptoms, he explains.

"It's their duty to report any adverse effects, just so people are aware of them," says Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

While NAION is scary, doctors say it's important to put the data in perspective. "It's extremely rare, but it can happen," Dr. Ali says. Given how much GLP-1s can help with blood sugar management, weight loss, and downstream health effects, Dr. Ali says that the risk of NAION is "not a reason not to seek these medications."

Dr. Rizzo agrees. "I essentially never discourage the general use of GLP-1 RA drugs," he says. "Ultimately, the risk-to-benefit assessment must be decided by the patient, but physicians should provide sufficient information to the patients to better inform their decisions."

People should stay aware of the risk without panicking, Dr. Youssefzadeh says. "It's also worth remembering that the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs—people with diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea—already carry a higher baseline risk for NAION, so the risk isn't starting from zero," he adds.

She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

#4832. This 377-Square-Foot Island Getaway in Denmark Is a Picture-Perfect Pint-Sized Retreat

A mini vacation home in Zealand, Denmark, is a particularly appealing retreat, no matter the season. With its rugged coastlines, forests, and small villages, the western side of Zealand offers an ideal setting for a break from everyday life. Nestled among trees is a tiny house that was designed to be as unobtrusive as possible. Its compact shape, natural color palette, and large windows allow it to blend almost seamlessly into the forest. Here, nature isn’t just right outside the door—it’s always present inside as well.

Surrounded by trees, this small wooden house in Denmark blends seamlessly with nature.

Named the EcoNeo House, the home was designed by the Danish architectural firm SAGA Space Architects, both as a family home and as a prototype for tiny house-style vacation homes. Although originally conceived as a summer house, the cottage has been insulated and heated, allowing it to be used even during colder weather. At only 377 square feet, it combines the essential features of a vacation home, sleeping up to six people. The design prioritizes a thoughtful use of the available space and forward-thinking architecture that blends into the landscape.

The spacious terrace is perfect for sunbathing and dining outdoors, especially in the summer.

Inside, the living and dining areas flow seamlessly into one another. Thanks to the large windows that offer views of the surrounding trees, there’s a connection between indoors and outdoors. The kitchen is set slightly apart, but opens up into the dining area, blending smoothly into the floor plan. Designed with functionality in mind, it’s still fully equipped with all the necessary appliances.

The dining area flows seamlessly into the kitchen. Additional storage space was created below the stairs on the left, which lead to the sleeping lofts.

Instead of breaking up the floor plan with additional walls, the architects made use of the home’s height: Stairs next to the kitchen lead to two sleeping lofts that offer a private retreat for up to four people. Storage was also a priority in the design. Items not needed on a daily basis can be stowed under the stairs, a clever solution that again makes the most of the small space.

Large windows let in plenty of natural light and create a connection between indoors and outdoors. Despite its compact size, the kitchen has all the necessary appliances.

There’s even a sauna, which can be converted into a sleeping space for two additional guests if needed. The generous window front offers a view of the surrounding landscape, while a cold plunge pool on the terrace is waiting for a refreshing dip afterward.

Through the sauna’s large window, you can enjoy the surrounding nature even while relaxing. It’s an appealing retreat, especially on chilly days. There’s also a cold plunge pool on the terrace.

The choice of materials complements the understated architecture. The floor’s wide Douglas fir planks introduce a warm color and vibrant grain. The use of wood is consistently carried through to other areas of the house, creating a visual connection between the living space and the sauna. Natural materials are also used in the bathroom, including Kolmården marble, a Swedish stone distinguished by its characteristic green hue.

Wood defines the interior and lends the rooms a natural warmth. Large windows bring the surrounding nature into the home, while the dining area is spacious even within the compact layout.

Together with the stones and the greenery outside, the result is a design that deliberately avoids contrasts and excess. “When designing the summer house, every detail was intended to reflect the harmony between sustainable innovation and timeless craftsmanship,” explains Niklas Munk-Andersen, architect and partner at SAGA Space Architects.

Beanbag chairs provide extra seating and blend harmoniously into the interior with their colors.

The Douglas fir floorboards also give the clean design a natural, tactile quality. The material is more than a surface design choice, instead it shapes the way that the rooms feel.

The bathroom features natural materials and Swedish marble finishes.

The sauna can also be converted into a sleeping area for two additional guests.

The compact design also has a positive impact on the home’s carbon footprint. According to calculations by SAGA Space Architects, the EcoNeo House produces approximately 386 pounds of CO₂ annually, whereas an average vacation home for six people is estimated to emit about 2,282 pounds. This means emissions are approximately 83% lower. In addition to the small living area, bio-based materials are the primary factor contributing to this difference.

The boundary between indoors and outdoors blurs, bringing nature into focus.

The architects also designed the construction process to be as efficient as possible by digitally planning the house, precisely prefabricating its individual components, and then assembling them on-site in a modular fashion. This approach not only simplified assembly but also minimized the impact on the site.

Thanks to its small footprint, this vacation home’s emissions are 83% lower than those of the average vacation home that can accommodate six people. In addition, the modular construction minimizes the impact on the natural environment.

The EcoNeo House demonstrates that sustainable construction isn’t just a matter of the materials used. The size of a building and how the available space is utilized also play a crucial role. Though it may sound small, 377 square feet can be perfectly sufficient for a getaway home—provided the floor plan, storage space, and amenities are all carefully designed.

Although primarily intended as a summer home, this small vacation home can also be enjoyed in colder months.

A skylight lets light into the upper sleeping lofts.

The small vacation home has two separate sleeping lofts accommodating four people.

#4831. Tesla Powerwall 3 now boosts heat pumps to store cheap solar as heat

Tesla has launched Heat Pump Optimization, a feature that lets the Powerwall 3 and three-phase Powerwall 3P tell a compatible heat pump when to run harder so a home can bank cheap or surplus solar energy as hot water.

It’s live in Europe only. Tesla hasn’t said anything about bringing it to the US or Canada, and the hardware standard it relies on barely exists on this side of the Atlantic.

According to Tesla’s support page for the feature, the Powerwall watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.

When it’s told to boost, the heat pump heats water beyond what the home needs right now, typically into a domestic hot water or buffer tank. That stored heat then carries the house through the expensive hours, when the heat pump can run less.

What triggers a boost depends on the Powerwall’s operating mode:

Tesla Energy summed it up on X last week: “Heat Pump Optimization allows your Powerwall to boost heating when there’s surplus solar or energy is inexpensive.”

There’s no cloud integration with heat pump brands here. It’s a wire.

The feature runs on SG-Ready (Smart Grid Ready), a label the German Heat Pump Association (BWP) introduced back in 2012 with 17 manufacturers. It uses two relay contacts on the heat pump to signal four operating states, from a utility block to a forced switch-on. Tesla only uses the “normal” and “boosted” recommendations.

Tesla’s requirements are pretty specific:

And there are limits. The signals are only recommendations, so the heat pump’s own thermostat settings can override them. Tesla also notes each signal has to be held for at least 10 minutes to comply with SG-Ready, and the feature drops back to normal during a power outage so the Powerwall can prioritize backup loads.

Oddly, there’s no on/off toggle in the Tesla app. Once it’s wired up, it’s on.

The math is what makes this interesting. A 300-liter hot water tank heated an extra 30°C holds about 10.5 kWh of thermal energy. With a heat pump running at a COP of 3, that takes only around 3.5 kWh of electricity to store.

So a tank most European heat pump homes already have can soak up a big chunk of midday solar without touching the lithium in the garage. That leaves the Powerwall’s 13.5 kWh free for the stuff that can’t be stored as heat.

The market is there too. Germany sold 299,000 heating heat pumps in 2025, up 55% year-over-year according to BWP, and they made up nearly half of all new heating systems sold in the country for the first time.

Tesla is also late to this. sonnen pushed a software update in 2023 that lets its sonnenBatterie run heat pumps off surplus solar, starting with NIBE units, and SG-Ready control has been a standard feature of German PV energy managers for years.

watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.

Heatpumps over here have been able to do this for years already.

And it's not one of two signals. Inverter controlled HP's enables control of the effect, and not just "normal or boost".

It’s the latest Europe-first move for Tesla Energy after it launched the Powerwall 3P with a native three-phase inverter earlier this year, aimed squarely at Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The company announced its 1 millionth Powerwall last year, and software like this is how it squeezes more value out of that installed base.

This is a smart, cheap feature, and it’s exactly the kind of thing that makes a home battery more valuable without adding a single cell.

Heat is the biggest energy load in most homes in cold climates, and water is about the cheapest storage medium there is. Using a battery’s brain to time the heat pump around solar and tariffs makes a lot more sense than discharging lithium to run a compressor at 6 p.m.

Home batteries are changing the economics of residential energy, and pairing them with solar (and smart loads like heat pumps) is the best way to get the most out of them. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. From Pilates to outdoor runs to heavy lifting sessions, I know exactly what separates a top you forget you’re wearing from one you can’t wait to peel off. For me, the best workout tops for women nail comfort, offer just enough support, and look flattering.

The last thing you want is an overly tight top that clips your movement (especially during yoga!), but it should still provide enough compression to hold you and the girls in, says Rebecca Stewart, CPT, a trainer and mobility coach. While you could make do with a regular cotton t-shirt during your workout sesh, it won't offer the same level of support, mobility, or sweat-wicking capabilities.

Finding the right workout top all comes down to personal preference. Because there are so many options to choose from—think T-shirts, tanks, and long-sleeve tops—we asked experts and tested tons of options ourselves to find styles we think will fit a wide range of needs and preferences. From lightweight, flowy options to compression shirts great for high-intensity workouts, our absolute favorite workout tops below are highlighted below.

Over the last few months I’ve tested a handful of workout tops and the Beyond Yoga Spacedye Slim Racerback Cropped Tank topped my list for a few reasons: It’s super comfortable (it won a spot for the softest bra in our Best Racerback Bras story!), has a built-in shelf bra, is size inclusive, and comes in a ton of vibrant and neutral shades.

It's basically the two-in-one bra and workout tank combo you didn’t know you needed. Made from the brand’s signature polyester and elastane blend, it’s the comfiest and most lightweight option I’ve ever worn. It feels like you're wearing nothing at all, but it still keeps the girls in place with a medium-level compression that’s perfect for light to moderate workouts. The cherry on top? It’s moisture-wicking, so it keeps you dry whether you’re working out or just running around on a hot day.

Our only gripe: If you have a bigger chest, you’ll probably want to layer a sports bra underneath for extra support. But if you're part of the itty bitty titty committee, you're good to go wearing this solo pretty much anywhere.

Read More: Beyond Yoga Spacedye Slim Racerback Tank Review

ICYMI, Amazon Essentials Activewear is where it’s at for affordable workout basics that rival the quality of some of the more luxe brands we’ve tried. The cotton, modal, and elastane blend feels thick, substantial, and smooth to the touch. It’s the kind of material that holds up well throughout repeated workouts and wash cycles, so you can keep this workout tee in constant rotation.

We also love the subtle crop length that isn’t too short or too long. It gives you room to move without showing too much skin, and has a semi-relaxed fit that perfectly skims the body. It’s extremely soft, but thanks to the touch of elastane in the fabric, it has ample stretch so you don’t feel constricted during overhead lifts or higher-impact workouts like running or HIIT.

The only con is that the white color can be slightly see-through. We suggest opting for a darker shade or wearing a flesh-toned bra underneath. The color options are also a little limited, but we love the slate gray and light blue options.

WH editors have tried a lot of workout tops over the years and agree that the Lululemon Ebb to Street Tank is a reliable favorite. It’s super soft, seamless, sweat-wicking, and ultra stretchy thanks to a comfortable blend of elastane and nylon. Plus, it offers just the right amount of support and coverage for low-impact workouts like Pilates, yoga, and walking.

The most convenient part: it has a built-in shelf bra, so you don’t have to wear a separate bra underneath (unless you want to for more support!). And, we found that it actually does keep us feeling covered and protected during low-impact exercise, which we didn’t find to be the case with other tanks that have built-in bras. Another pro? The longer length of this top (it hits at the hip) keeps us feeling locked in and covered during workouts where we don’t want a ton of stomach showing.

“I love how versatile this top is, along with its longer length and the buttery-soft blend of nylon and elastane,” says trainer Kristina Earnest, CPT, founder of Kristina Earnest On Demand. This is her go-to top when she's working out at home, and she wears it under a sweater for her cold weather errands. It feels incredibly comfortable thanks to its seamless racerback design—no pesky straps, seams, or tightness to get in the way during your sweat session. However, you should note that because there are no adjustable straps, you can't customize the fit of this tank.We put this tank to the test during a variety of workouts, like HIIT training and running, and found that it’s not the best choice for high-intensity training. We noticed that it didn’t do a great job of holding the breasts in place during high-impact moves and felt the need for more padding and compression. But based on our extensive testing, it's difficult to find a tank with high-impact support. That's why we recommend pairing this with our favorite high-impact sports bra, the Under Armour Infinity 2.0 High Sports Bra.

This tank is meant to be worn over your favorite sports bra as an added layer of coverage. The loose, cropped fit is easy to throw on, and the round neck with the knotted side detail adds a touch of style. Our fave part about this tank? The cotton material is super breathable, so you never feel overheated or constricted like you would with a tighter top.

“I love that this top isn’t too tight,” says Jacqueline Kasen, CPT, trainer and senior director of group fitness at Anatomy. “It’s super comfortable and loose whether you’re running or lifting, but it still stays in place without bunching up.” Plus, it holds its shape after multiple washes and never pills or frays, making it as durable as it is functional.

The tank is made with cotton, but it also has a bit of spandex woven throughout, which makes it stretchy and not too sturdy. This is essential during workouts, as you want your top to move with you instead of against you at the gym.

We noticed that the shirt can look a bit boxy if you go too oversized, so we recommend sizing down for a more flattering, snug fit.

This short-sleeve workout top from Under Armour is a game changer for high-intensity exercise since it offers both compression and cooling technology. It’s designed as a baselayer to keep you protected under your sports gear (by preventing pinching and chafing), but we love to wear it on its own as a temperature-regulating, sweat-wicking, ultra-lightweight workout top.

This t-shirt has an ultra-tight, compressive fit (which can help with circulation and muscular endurance), but it is super thin and made with the brand's HeatGear fabric to keep you from overheating. It’s made from polyester for a smooth, lightweight feel, plus elastane for a generous amount of stretch. We love that this top is breathable and moisture-wicking, so even though it’s on the tighter side, it doesn’t feel like you’re wearing anything. Whether you’re lifting heavy or doing sprints outdoors, this top is perfect for keeping you cool, dry, and comfortable.

However, this top (like most compressive gear) might not be the best option for lower-impact exercise or workouts that require lots of stretching and bending—like yoga or Pilates. We generally opt for looser, softer fits for these workouts and stick to tighter tops for strength training and cardio.

Listen, I love a cute lil workout set as much as the next Pilates princess, but sometimes I don’t want to bare my entire midriff. That’s where an oversized workout top like this one comes in clutch. I especially love it in white because it's just a touch see-through, so it lets me show off my matching sports bra and workout short combo without feeling exposed. It’s also perfect for those days when I feel a little bloated and just need something loose-fitting that won’t emphasize my stomach.

Unlike the other workout tops you’ll find here, this tee is made from 100% cotton. The natural fiber is not exactly known for its high-performance abilities at the gym (it doesn’t wick sweat very well), but the thinner construction and super boxy fit help keep things super airy. I wore it for an outdoor workout over the summer and felt cool and comfortable—well, as much as you can while doing burpees.

It’s also just a really cute shape. I love the sleeves, which, despite being those of a t-shirt, hit at about the elbow, giving it a really laidback feel. I love it for working out or for throwing on over my skin-tight sets to and from Pilates, but I also find myself grabbing it day-to-day for errands and casual outings. I frequently throw it on over a bright tank styled with some longline biker shorts and comfy sneaks for a cool-girl fit that basically feels like I’m wearing pajamas.

As with any oversized workout tee, it might not be the wisest choice for HIIT workouts or anything super tactical. The billowing sleeves and loose fit could get caught on equipment or flop over your face while bending or jumping.

An open-back top is not only a super stylish choice, but it helps keep you cool as a cucumber during sweaty workouts too. I especially love this top for hot Pilates when I want as little fabric against my skin as possible. And since it has built-in padding (that doesn’t shift around in the wash!), I can literally just wear this on its own to yoga, Pilates, strength training, or other low-impact workouts.

I have worn this during my more intense exercise like an Orangetheory class or while running, and it does offer enough support for me (as someone who teeters between a C cup and a D cup). But if you have a larger chest size, it might be best to reserve this top for low-impact movement or layer it over your favorite sports bra.

Nike’s Dri-FIT tech (a blend of nylon and spandex) is also a major pro. It feels sleek and smooth against the skin but also helps move sweat away from the body. When I leave an intense workout class (even a heated one), it’s noticeable how much less sweat I have sitting between my skin and my workout top when I reach for this one, which is huge for me, since I’ve been struggling with eczema that gets worse with heat and sweat.

The material is also suuuper stretchy and comfortable, and never gets in the way of any kind of movement, whether that’s mat Pilates or an intense upper-body session at the gym. It’s also really lightweight so it feels nearly like a second skin and never requires adjustments mid-workout.

This tank from Gymshark pairs perfectly with the brand’s bestselling leggings. Like the leggings, this tank is nearly seamless—the only seams are along the bottom hem, but they are super flat and don’t cause any rubbing or chafing when up against the skin.

I love that the stretchy, smooth fabric (made of 96% nylon and 4% elastane) is basically sweat-proof and dries super quickly. That’s because nylon is a synthetic fabric that’s hydrophobic (i.e. it resists the penetration of water), so this top is great for wicking moisture away from the body during intense workouts.

Not only that, but it’s super cute, too. I love the square neckline and the length that hits right at the hip bones. It also has a built-in shelf bra to help support and lift the girls for a more flattering shape and a little extra protection against bounce during your workouts. It might not be enough support for larger chest sizes during high-intensity movement, but for smaller chests and moderate activity, it does the trick.

We’ve all been in those super stuffy gyms. When I start overheating during a workout, all I want is to be in a sports bra. But I’m not always comfortable showing my stomach. That’s where the Wild Thing Bra comes in. With its longline fit, which ends just above my belly button for slightly more coverage than a standard sports bra, the top leaves me feeling cool and comfortable at the gym.

And, of course, it’s super cute, thanks to the ruching in the center of the bra. I find this detail really flattering—it gives my stomach a snatched look when I wear it. While it doesn’t offer a ton of support since it’s on the lighter side, it provides decent compression for my higher intensity workouts. Its lightweight design and stylish details make it perfect for pairing with leggings at the gym, but I’ve also seen it styled with trousers or jeans for a sporty yet upscale vibe.

Worried about the lighter colors looking sheer? Don’t be! All styles come with removable cups to cover your girls, which is also helpful because you can take them out when you wash the bra. Speaking of washing, we find that this bra holds up well after multiple washes and never pills or changes in elasticity and shape.

One thing to keep in mind is that the straps aren’t adjustable, which can be a bit frustrating since it means you can’t customize the fit. I also wish it came in more colors.

This tank won the top spot in our Best Workout Tank Tops story for a few reasons: It's super flattering, never rides up, is compressive, supportive, and sweat-wicking.

We tested this ribbed tank across many different workouts—running, yoga, lifting, and HIIT—and we found that it never moves or rides up. And, we love that it’s a tighter spandex tank with high compression, as it holds us in all the right places and doesn’t allow for any boob bounce. It doesn’t have a built-in bra, but it’s tight enough to hold the chest in place.

It's also super moisture-wicking. WH assistant fashion editor Rose Lauture wore this during an intense workout and said there were no sweat stains, no matter which color she wore, thanks to the soft nylon. Because it's moisture-wicking, it also does a great job at preventing body odor.

This option offers some pretty solid support for not having a built-in bra (it's all about the compression!). However, it is made for medium support, so we like to wear an extra bra underneath this tank from time to time when our workouts get extra intense.

Stewart’s pro tip? For high-impact or high-intensity workouts, look for materials that are shiny and smooth to reduce chafing and wick sweat. For lower-intensity workouts, look for matte fabrics that have a soft, buttery texture for comfort and flexibility.

Should your workout top be loose or tight? While it does come down to personal preference, there are pros and cons to each. Tighter tops don’t get in the way of movement as much as a looser top might: they often feel more secure and supportive. But if you find looser tops more comfortable, they can certainly work for nearly every workout except for those involving a Pilates reformer (where loose fabric can easily get caught) or other equipment like cable machines.

Some workout tops have built-in shelf bras or bra pad inserts, but this can be a “love it or hate it” situation, says Stewart. For bigger busts or high-intensity activities, a built-in bra may not provide enough support, so you might need an extra sports bra underneath. However, for smaller busts, we find that they provide ample support for light- and medium-intensity workouts. “A built-in bra should feel supportive and not bothersome and shouldn’t be too tight or digging in to restrict your movement,” says Stewart.

There are tons of workout tops out there, so even finding the absolute best options to test was difficult. When I began the November 2026 update of this article, I revisited our original February 2024 story to see which of the picks our team is still wearing. Some of them are still team favorites, but I went back to the drawing board and asked fitness experts and stylists, including style contributors Kristen Saladino, Rose Lauture, and Lily Wohlner, which workout tops they were loving. From there, I removed the picks that we are no longer wearing and added the options we’ve been reaching for the most.

I made sure that the final picks on this list were options that we wear across all sorts of activities, from compressive options perfect for HIIT workout classes to lightweight, flowy tops we like for lounging or lower-impact exercise. Some of the contenders on this list come in tons of different colors and styles, have built-in bras, and are made with the highest-quality materials for their price points.

#4829. The Surprising Staying Power of Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy

A24’s Club Kid makes the case for the comedy’s unlikely legacy—and social relevance—in 2026.

EARLY ON IN Jordan Firstman’s dramedy Club Kid, druggie-with-a-heart-of-gold Peter has to shepherd his surprise 10-year-old son through an apartment party. Despite knowing each other for just a few hours, the club promoter and his child hold hands as he guides the way through the bacchanal. It’s a metaphor—what isn’t these days?—and it’s also kind of a recreation of a key sequence in Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy.

In that movie, 5-year-old Julian “Frankenstein” McGrath (played by young Dylan and Cole Sprouse) holds his hand aloft before he steps off the sidewalk, looking for help from his newfound father.

Replace McDonald’s breakfasts with coke and ketamine (plus a Charlie Kirk reference), and A24’s Club Kid is the clear heir apparent to the 1999 Sandler comedy. I’m far from the first person to make the connection. IndieWire’s David Ehrlich’s first-impression response was to ask: “What if A24 made a gay Big Daddy?”

It may seem like an odd movie for a brand like A24 to mirror. However, Big Daddy is somehow the film from the peak Sandler run that has had the longest shelf life. In fact, it may be the late ’90s–early 2000s comedy with the best depiction of the 2026 way of life. For better—or for worse.

Despite the fact that it was a hit at the box office, Big Daddy was reviled at the time of its release, even winning Sandler a Razzie Award for Worst Actor.

And, sure, it’s not the most elegant film—with its near-incessant Hooters jabs and Rob Schneider’s catastrophic accent—but still, it’s managed to stick around in the public consciousness for nearly 30 years. And it’s not just Ehrlich and I who think so.

“I particularly loved Big Daddy. That was my number one,” Paul Thomas Anderson said on an episode of The Bill Simmons Podcast in 2017 when asked about casting Sandler in his film Punch-Drunk Love. “It was a little bit more polished; it was able to be sincere and [mix in] the crazy fucking dirty shit that Sandler likes to do and got the mix really right.”

In Club Kid, promoter Peter (Firstman, who wrote, directed, and stars) somehow ends up in charge of a precocious kid while flailing in both romance and his career. Peter, like Sonny, has to instantly shift his lifestyle, one that only functions when you have little to care for, including yourself. Both protagonists need an act of God to abandon their early-30s doldrums.

And honestly, it’s a sentiment that a lot of people my age (including myself) can relate to.

At the tail end of October, The New York Times published a story (which, thankfully, my parents haven’t sent to me yet) titled “Can’t Afford a Home. Can’t Afford a Baby. Can’t Afford Life. This Is 30.” The gist is that millennials feel burned out now that they know they’re unlikely to achieve the luxuries earlier generations enjoyed.

“In the past, the idea was that you would check all these boxes by 30, give or take. But the more I think about it, so much of that is incredibly out of reach,” says one source in the article. Even decades ago, Sonny Koufax would have probably agreed with the article, before ripping out part of the newspaper to clean up some spilled milk next to his third bowl of cereal of the day. Both films find the hearts at the center of their respective protagonists’ messy, work-in-progress stories. Is there anything more 2026 than that?

When you watch Big Daddy in 2026, you almost forget how much of a schmuck—but vulnerable too—Sandler allowed Sonny to be. I was pleasantly surprised that Sandler ultimately loses his chance at raising Julian by himself. It’s a small, complicated victory for a movie that uses a schlocky, heartfelt monologue about fathers to reach a contrived moral coda, but we’ll take our wins where we can get them.

Greg is a freelance writer and AMC Stubs A-List member when he’s not the Senior Digital Producer at Golf Digest. You can read his movie reviews and existential crises on his Aerial Shot newsletter. He’s sorry in advance if you liked something that he didn’t.

#4828. 007 Off Duty: 10 Photos of Former James Bond Actors at Home

For a secret agent, James Bond generates a remarkable amount of public discussion. Barely a day goes by without fresh speculation about who will be the next actor to take on the role of 007. Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O’Connor are among the names linked to the role, with recent reports suggesting the search has reached final screen tests.

Whoever takes over will join the small group who have played the part since Sean Connery’s debut in Dr. No in 1962. Away from the screen, the homes of these former James Bond actors reveal more about the men in the dinner jackets. These archival photographs find them settling into family life and indulging interests that occasionally followed them onto set. Below, find a little domestic distraction while we wait for the next Bond to introduce himself.

Sean Connery relaxing in his ground-floor basement flat in NW5.

Photographed at home in England in 1955, Connery is still around seven years away from his first appearance as James Bond in this shapshot. His surroundings are modest, with little suggestion of the polished interiors his screen alter ego was about to frequent. Connery established the role of Bond across six films in during the 1960s and early 1970s.

Landing the role of James Bond required a little wardrobe planning on George Lazenby’s part. According to the official Bond website, the former model bought an unused suit made for Connery, then visited his predecessor’s barber at the Dorchester to request the same haircut. Producer Cubby Broccoli happened to be in the neighboring chair.

George Lazenby pictured at his home in Kensington, London, 1973.

His only appearance as 007 was in the 1969 film On Her Majesty's Secret Service. It gave Bond one of his most personal storylines, with Diana Rigg playing his ill-fated bride, Tracy. By the time of the Kensington photograph shown above in February 1973, Lazenby had already left the role. Seated with papers in hand, he is surrounded by books, records and a guitar propped beside the sofa. The glass-topped coffee table is crowded with objects, including a decorative horse’s head, while a substantial wooden cabinet provides storage behind him. Later that year, Roger Moore made his Bond debut in Live and Let Die.

Roger Moore reading the dictionary at his home in Los Angeles, circa 1955.

Roger Moore had yet to order his first on-screen Bond martini when he was photographed at home reading a dictionary, while working as a television actor.

Roger Moore kissing his wife, Welsh singer Dorothy Squires, outside their home in Bexley Heath, London, in 1957.

He married Welsh singer Dorothy Squires in 1953, and they lived primarily at The Mount—a mansion on Wansunt Road in Old Bexley, Kent.

The couple divorced in 1968, and a year later, Moore married Luisa Mattioli. Sherwood House in Denham, located close to Pinewood Studios, served as the couple's base during Moore's first three Bond films. In his autobiography, he described the property as “near London and perfect for a growing family.”

Its appeal extended to 11 acres of grounds, which included a tennis court, heated swimming pool and greenhouses when the house was advertised for £5 million in 2015.

When he finally took on Bond's on-screen persona, Timothy Dalton was well-prepared for the role.

Producers considered Timothy Dalton for Bond early in his career, but he felt too young for the role. When he eventually signed on for The Living Daylights in 1986, he reread Fleming’s novels to prepare for a more serious interpretation of the character.

Pierce Brosnan at home in Los Angeles in 1983.

Pierce Brosnan was making his name in Remington Steele when he posed at his Los Angeles home in June 1983, but his introduction to the world of Bond had come through his first wife, actress Cassandra Harris. She appeared in For Your Eyes Only, and visiting her on location in Corfu brought him into the producers’ orbit. Brosnan was offered the role in 1986, but was prevented from taking it due to his television commitments at the time. His debut in GoldenEye came almost a decade later, in 1995.

Pierce Brosnan playing pool with his son, Sean, at their Los Angeles home in 1992.

This 1992 photographs show Brosnan playing guitar on the sofa, shooting pool with his eight-year-old son Sean, and entertaining two dogs in the garden. Cream sofas and floral upholstery adorn the living room, while arched windows and white shutters open the space to the surrounding greenery. Taken the year after Harris died of ovarian cancer, the photographs capture Brosnan bringing up their family before Bond transformed his career.

Pierce Brosnan with his dogs outside of their Los Angeles home in 1992.

Painting had become a creative outlet for the star during Harris’s illness. Having trained as a commercial artist before acting, Brosnan returned to it in the late 1980s, recalling on his website: “I started painting again and out came every colour.” By the time he became Bond, painting was so sufficiently embedded in his life that his dressing room at Leavesden doubled as a studio during GoldenEye.

Daniel Craig attends the Bond 25 film launch at Ian Fleming's Home, GoldenEye, in Montego Bay, Jamaica, 2019.

For this final entry, the front door stays closed. Of all the former James Bond actors, Daniel Craig represents a more guarded approach to sharing domestic life. His wife, actress Rachel Weisz, explained the couple’s position in a 2012 conversation with British Vogue: “I think it’s pretty ordinary to think that marriage is private and sacred.”

Speculation over who will inherit Craig's martini glass keeps his name in the headlines even after his departure.

#4827. Cadillac’s most affordable EV just got a bit cheaper

The 2027 Cadillac Optiq offers up to 317 miles of range, a massive 33″ infotainment screen, an NACS charge port, and now it’s a bit more affordable.

The Optiq first went on sale in 2025 as Cadillac’s entry-level electric SUV, starting at $54,390. For the 2026 model year, the Optiq arrived as GM’s first electric vehicle with a built-in NACS port and added a new rear-wheel-drive (RWD) powertrain.

Thanks to the new RWD option, the 2026 Optiq (see our review) was also slightly less expensive, with prices starting at $52,395.

While GM initially said the 2027 Cadillac Optiq would start at $52,695, prices on its website have been updated and are now slightly lower.

The base 2027 Cadillac Optiq Luxury RWD is now listed at $51,790, or $905 less than the initial price announced months ago. The Luxury AWD trim is also $905 cheaper, starting at $55,290.

Meanwhile, the Sport trim now starts at $52,395 for RWD and $55,895 for AWD, both $900 less than before.

The higher-spec Optiq Premium Luxury, Premium Sport, and V-Series trims remain at the price GM initially announced.

The 2027 Cadillac Optiq offers up to 317 miles of range in the RWD models and 303 miles with AWD. All models come with a standard 33″ Horizon Display infotainment screen, a 19-speaker AKG Studio Audio System, GM’s Super Cruise hands-free driver-assist technology, and a native NACS charge port.

Upgrading to AWD costs an extra $3,500. The Premium Luxury and Premium Sport add standard features including a Head-Up Display, ventilated and lumbar massaging front seats, and a rear cargo cover.

The high-performance 2027 Optiq-V starts at $69,295 and delivers a Cadillac-estimated 519 lb-ft of torque and 650 horsepower in Velocity MaX Mode,

How does the Cadillac Optiq stack up against the Tesla Model Y? The base Tesla Model Y RWD starts at $39,990 with up to 321 miles of range, while the AWD version costs $41,990 and gets up to 294 miles.

The Tesla Model Y Premium RWD starts at $45,990 with up to 355 miles of range, while the Premium AWD starts at $49,990 and has 327 miles of range.

Had the opportunity to drive the Optiq as a loaner while my Lyriq was in for service. I truly liked how it handled but I did find what I call a safety issue due to its design. The A pillar has an extra vertical piece and that combined with really no usable visual space forward and the side mirror create a blind spot when wanting to make a left turn on dark roads. No problem in the city where there is light. If GM would have added front side lighting when making a turn that could have been eliminated. Would have seriously looked at the Optiq for the next vehicle but that blind spot is a show stopper for me. Well that, and the fact the Optiq does not support CarPlay.

Inside, the base Tesla Model Y has a 16″ QHD touchscreen and 7-speaker audio system. The Premium model gains a 15-speaker Tesla Audio System with a subwoofer, plus an 8″ second-row touchscreen.

The two are nearly the same size, but the Tesla Model Y offers slightly more rear legroom and cargo capacity than the Cadillac Optiq.

#4826. Hardee’s gets EV fast charging – with Carl’s Jr. locations to follow

EV drivers have a new reason to pull into Hardee’s. Energized EV has opened four fast-charging ports at a restaurant in Temple, Georgia, kicking off a planned rollout at Hardee’s and Carl’s Jr. locations across the US.

There’s no site count or rollout schedule yet, but the first location is open with both NACS and CCS1 connectors.

The chargers are at 587 Carrollton Street in Temple. The site has two dual-port XCharge C7 DC fast chargers, each rated at 240 kW, for a total of four charging ports. Monta provides the chargers’ software. XCharge says the C7 adjusts power output between its two connectors, and both NACS and CCS1 connectors are on offer.

“Adding charging at our restaurants gives EV drivers a convenient place to stop, recharge, and enjoy a meal,” said Mike Darger, vice president of facilities and maintenance at CKE Restaurants. “We look forward to building on this first opening as more locations come online across the country.”

Energized EV says more Hardee’s and Carl’s Jr. sites are planned across the US, with president and CEO Devin Grandis calling Temple “the beginning of a much larger expansion.”

Energy & Environmental Design Services LLC (E&EDS) is the program’s exclusive installer. Its services include charging infrastructure design, installation, and maintenance, as well as electrical contracting.

Then there's the saga of how to keep the lazy and over-sized patrons from parking their 2004 Explorer in those spaces.

Gas stations with food offered and restaurants with charging offered are similar yet different. Instead of eating while you gas up, we can now charge up while we eat. The latter being the better option.

Energized EV’s approach is to install chargers where drivers already stop, whether they’re running errands or taking a longer road trip. But we’ll need the next locations and opening dates to see how useful this restaurant charging network will become. The announcement doesn’t list charging prices for Temple.

A dry, itchy scalp can seriously mess with your day-to-day life. Beyond the maddening urge to scratch, there's the embarrassing component: dandruff and big white flakes studding your strands. And while dermatologists say that a dry, flaking scalp may be a sign of a medical condition called seborrheic dermatitis (this requires a prescription treatment like Zoryve), the best scalp moisturizers—hydrating shampoos for dry scalp, conditioners, and serums—can help.

"I always recommend starting with a gentle, sulfate-free shampoo that cleanses without stripping the scalp of its natural oils and following that up with a hydrating conditioner," says Ross Kopelman, MD, a hair transplant surgeon at Kopelman Hair Restoration in New York City. You can then follow that up with a leave-in treatment or a scalp oil to really lock in moisture.

It's also a good idea to limit hair washing to two to three times a week. "I suggest washing your hair with lukewarm water instead of hot and avoiding excessive heat styling, which can make things worse," Kopelman says. Before adding a few scalp moisturizers to your routine, here's what you should consider before shopping.

#4822. The BMW iX is sold out, but you might like what takes its place even more

BMW is saying goodbye to the iX. With the 2026 model essentially sold out, BMW is preparing to introduce its replacement, which already looks like a big upgrade.

The iX went on sale in the US in 2022 as BMW’s first dedicated electric SUV. After a short four-year run, BMW confirmed earlier this year that it was discontinuing the iX in the US after the 2026 model year to make room for its next-generation of fully electric vehicles.

BMW didn’t take long to sell through inventory, with 2026 iX models essentially sold out in the US.

The iX landing page now redirects you to the new BMW X5 instead. According to online auto research firm CarsDirect, about 10 new iX models remain nationwide.

BMW’s Neue Klasse vehicles, starting with the new 2027 iX3, mark a step change from its previous EVs.

At the center is the Neue Klasse platform, which introduces BMW’s sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive, new batteries, and an 800-volt electrical architecture.

BMW said the new Gen6 eDrive system delivers 30% higher charging speeds and driving range than its previous system, with some models seeing an even greater increase.

The 2027 iX3 50 xDrive, BMW’s first Neue Klasse vehicle, starts at $61,500 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 434 miles. In comparison, the 2026 iX xDrive 60 had an EPA range of up to 364 miles.

While the iX3 is a smaller, compact electric SUV compared to the iX, BMW is preparing to launch the iX5 as a more direct replacement.

The gas-powered 2027 X5 40 xDrive is now on sale, starting at $72,100, but BMW is expected to launch the electric iX5 in early 2027.

A few weeks ago, BMW put the new iX5 60 xDrive to the test at an international media event in Southern California to show just how fast it can charge.

During the event, the new iX5 hit a peak of 464 kW. BMW said that with up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes. To charge the battery from 10% to 80% takes just 22 minutes.

Using a 144 kWh battery, BMW said the electric SUV will offer up to an estimated 435 miles of range on a single charge.

The iX5 is powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, delivering a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW says it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 will be an upgrade from the iX, adopting BMW’s Neue Klasse design. The setup includes a 17.9″ navigation touchscreen and the new BMW Panoramic Vision that spans the windshield. You can also opt to add the optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.

The new drive platform is a huge improvement. Personally I'm glad to see it in the new i3 since I don't think everyone needs a 3-ton SUV.

Measuring 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, the iX5 is slightly longer and taller than the outgoing iX, with more of a traditional SUV design.

BMW is expected to open orders for the new iX5 60 xDrive this month, starting at $79,800, with a full launch in early 2027. It will be BMW’s first fully electric vehicle built in the US.

Production is set to begin at BMW’s Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina by the end of the year, with the first deliveries expected in early 2027.

The cost of the Lifestraw Go here is a little elevated, but you are paying for the special filter. You do need to change the LifeStraw filter inside about every 60 days, so that's an extra cost. The payoff though, from what our editors discovered, is the peace of mind you get filling up your water bottle at a public water fountain or from tap water that comes out of a sink.

Grab this water bottle if you're looking for a filtered option with excellent design. There are times when you can’t fully trust your water source but this vessel affords peace of mind (and no bickering of the gut).

To say these bottles were tested is an understatement. Over the course of several years, various Men's Health editors and I put them to work—like, overtime. We paired them up with the most active members of our team, allowing us to get a clean picture of just how well these bottles perform. Hot weather, cold weather, in the gym, out on the trail, on the saddle of a bike, on plane rides, or just commuting; we brought them everywhere.

Throughout the process, we paid close attention to various attributes. Obviously, we wanted a water bottle that looks good. But more importantly, we wanted a water bottle that made staying hydrated easy, thoughtless, and perhaps even enjoyable. We analyzed design, material, size, and special features. We waded through reputable reviews and talked up insiders in the outdoors recreation and sporting worlds for their takes. And of course, we looked at price.

In the end, the Yeti has won us over on all fronts. Durable, lightweight, packable, and super affordable, it has been a favorite among many testers since it released in 2022. But several others came close, offering different traits like filtration, improved insulation, or more sophisticated lids.

Some people prefer wide-mouth tops on their water bottles for faster drinking, while others prefer a spout design that's much smaller and easier to sip. Really it comes down to preference, but there are spout designs we tested that are more enjoyable to drink from than others. Do keep in mind that lots of companies make tops that are interchangeable in case you want to switch to a different design.

To avoid any contamination of plastics, most water bottles we reviewed came in a metal design. There are some plastic water bottles we tested, however, that were BPA-free and we found to not have any impact on taste. Our top-tested water bottle from Yeti is actually made from BPA-free plastic. Our editors have tested this water bottle for nearly two years and have found no issues with taste or with material breakdown from a dishwasher.

Material also dictates temperature retention, with things like double-insulated stainless steel keeping things nice and chilled for long periods of time. Plastic tends to not insulate quite as well, but can be quite durable (and recycled). Keep this in mind as you weigh how important an ice-cold pull of water is to you.

How much water are you going to need? Capacity is a vital consideration, as you might just be looking for a little hydration while at work (where you can continue to refill when necessary) or be out and about all weekend at the campground, potentially away from a water source. Less volume is just fine for quicker outings or when you want to be streamlined, like on a bike. But you'll be wanting additional capacity for, say, lengthy conferences, road trips, or exhausting workout routines.

There are a few water bottles we selected thanks to special features our editors love. Lifestraw, for example, provides some of the best water filtration you can buy. The fact Lifestraw discreetly hides its filter behind a stainless steel body is a huge reason why we featured it on our list. The same goes for the Camelbak Podium, as its insulated body and cap and spout design make it especially suitable for indoor gym settings.

Yes. A reusable bottle is easier on the planet for that very reason—it's reusable. Single-use plastic is wasteful stuff and, worse, it does not decompose, likely ending up in the ocean and your food supply chain (not to mention turning into microplastic). Going with a bottle like the ones listed here does require some energy and inputs upfront, but because it's your long-term bottle (don't go losing it now), the carbon footprint is less.

You can take it a step further by purchasing a bottle made with responsibly sourced materials, sometimes even made from up-cycled or recycled materials. Look for non-BPA (a bad chemical) options and preferably ones that use very little if no plastic. Glass and stainless steel are generally easier on Mother Earth. And be good to yourself by keeping the thing clean and sterile.

Here's the thing about mold: It likes wet environments. You know, like inside of your water bottle. It's a repulsive thought, but some of that gunk buildup in your vessel might just be mold. Don't fret, you can clean the thing.

Now, it would take a fair amount of mold to sicken the average person but regardless, a clean water bottle is just worth having. Wash your bottle daily, either in the dishwasher if it's permitted or by hand, ideally with hot water and a scrub to get into those nooks and crannies—water bottle brushes are a great tool.

Occasionally, consider a more intense clean. Do to the bottle as you might to your coffee maker, soaking it in a mix of vinegar and water. Even the occasional boiling water soak will help keep the bottle pristine.

#4819. Healthy on the Outside: The Silent Risk Dr. Nancy Snyderman Never Saw Coming

Nancy L. Snyderman, MD, spent decades helping millions of Americans understand their health. But when it came to her own health, it was a nudge from a friend that finally pushed her to get the care she really needed.

Nancy L. Snyderman, MD, began her career caring for one patient at a time. After medical school, Nancy became a board-certified surgeon, working at academic medical centers, and she kept running into the same gap: the distance between what doctors knew and what patients actually understood about their own health. Television, she realized, could help close it. “A big part of being a doctor, for me, was putting humanity back into medicine,” she says. So she traded caring for one patient at a time for caring for all Americans.

For nearly three decades, Americans welcomed Nancy into their homes through their televisions. As a chief medical correspondent, she covered wide ranging medical topics and traveled the world extensively, reporting from many of the world’s most-troubled areas. Every day, she expertly translated complex medical news into easily digestible—and actionable—information for people across America.

“I spent my whole career being the person who talked about health to help others,” she says. “I never thought I’d be the one in need of help.”

Nancy has always been active. Even now, she hikes, travels and keeps up with her young grandchildren. But being active and feeling good doesn’t always mean you’re healthy. No one knows this better than Nancy, who had no symptoms of heart disease before her diagnosis. It started when she was still a national medical correspondent, working on a story on CT angiograms and a then-new test that provided a coronary artery calcium (CAC) score. As part of her report, Nancy had the scan done herself and her score came back at 100. “I thought, ‘Oh my gosh, this is great, I aced this test’,” she says—only to learn that acing it means a score of zero.

What is a CAC Scan?A coronary artery calcium (CAC) scan is an imaging test that measures the amount of calcified plaque built up in the heart's arteries.1 It can help doctors and patients understand cardiovascular risk—even before symptoms appear.1

At the same time, she was struggling to keep her LDL-C, or low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, often called “bad” cholesterol, in check. High LDL-C is one of the leading risk factors for a heart attack or stroke, but also one of the most modifiable.2 To lower her LDL-C, Nancy had been taking statins—which are a commonly prescribed class of LDL-C lowering medication—for decades. “I knew what to do, and I thought I was doing the right things,” she says. “But I was never able to really get my bad cholesterol to my doctor-recommended level.”

What finally changed everything was a conversation. After reconnecting with an old friend, who also happens to be a cardiac nurse, Nancy mentioned her CAC score and stubborn LDL-C. Her friend insisted that Nancy see a new cardiologist. After some additional testing, the results were nothing Nancy ever expected to hear: severe coronary artery disease, with significant blockages in the arteries feeding her heart.

What is LDL-C?LDL-C stands for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol—often called “bad” cholesterol. When too much of it builds up in the blood, it can settle into artery walls, narrowing them and raising the risk of a heart attack or stroke over time.2

“My diagnosis was a huge wake-up call,” she says. “I thought I was doing the right things, but even I, as a physician, needed an advocate.” She’s quick to point out why that mattered: “A lot of the risks women face with heart disease can be managed,” she adds, “but only if we understand them and speak up for ourselves.”

Nancy’s experience is far more common than many women realize. Heart disease remains the leading cause of death for women in the United States3—yet only about half (56%) of women recognize it as their number one threat.3 “One of the most dangerous things about heart disease is how quietly it can develop,” says Sirisha Vadali, MD, a board-certified cardiologist in Scottsdale, Arizona. “It can progress silently, even when you feel completely healthy,4 and women in particular may not have the obvious warning signs we’ve all been taught to watch for.”

So much of that hidden risk traces back to a single number: LDL-C. When there’s too much of this “bad” cholesterol circulating, it doesn’t just sit in the blood. It works its way into the artery walls and builds up as a sticky plaque, narrowing them and raising the risk of a heart attack or stroke over time.5,6 “It isn’t only how high your LDL-C is today,” Dr. Vadali says. “It’s how high it has been, and for how long. The longer it’s too high, the more cardiovascular risk accumulates.”⁵

For Nancy, the lesson was humbling: expertise is not immunity. “You can be the most informed person in the room and still miss a health warning in yourself,” she says. It sometimes takes a push from a loved one to take the necessary action.

After her diagnosis, Nancy did exactly what she had spent years urging her viewers to do: she partnered with her cardiologist and built a plan. Together, they assessed her individual risk factors and set a clear target for her LDL-C to help lower her cardiovascular risk.

Getting there was more challenging than Nancy realized. “Despite standard treatment, diet, and exercise, my LDL-C was still too high, and we needed to lower it to my doctor-recommended LDL-C goal,” she says.

That gap—between lower and a guideline-recommended target—is one Dr. Vadali sees constantly. “When it comes to LDL-C, lower is better, but ‘lower’ isn’t the same as reaching the guideline-recommended goal for your unique risk factors,” she says.

What are the Guideline-Recommended Goals?The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia recommends specific LDL-C goals based on individual risk. For example, below 70 mg/dL for people with diabetes and multiple cardiovascular risk factors, and below 55 mg/dL for those with cardiovascular disease at very high risk.7,*

“Knowing your LDL-C number—and talking with your doctor about what’s right for you—is one of the first steps toward understanding your risk level,” Dr. Vadali adds.

She’s also quick to retire a persistent myth. “For a lot of people, especially those already at increased cardiovascular risk, diet and exercise alone may not be enough to get LDL-C to the guideline-recommended goal,” Dr. Vadali says. “That’s not a personal failing. It’s biology. Sometimes the body needs additional help, and that’s worth a conversation with your doctor.”

For Nancy, that additional help became part of her plan. Working with her cardiologist, she started treatment with REPATHA® (evolocumab) to help lower her LDL-C and reduce her risk of a major cardiovascular event.

Repatha® is an injectable prescription medicine used:

Please see additional Important Safety Information below and full Prescribing Information.

These days, treatment is a welcome part of Nancy’s routine. “Every two weeks, I give myself an injection and have built a small ritual around it as part of my treatment plan to help keep my LDL-C at the goal my doctor recommended,” she says. “I can take it in the comfort of my own home or on the go† which is a treatment that can fit into my routine.”

Nancy is careful to say her path is her own. “I’m sharing my experience as a patient, but everyone’s situation is different,” she says. “What mattered was working with my doctor to figure out what was right for me. That’s what I want for every woman reading this to consider.”

Dr. Vadali says REPATHA is a treatment she has consistently recommended for appropriate patients. “I prescribe REPATHA because we know it starts working quickly,” she says. “For high-risk patients, keeping LDL-C lower will help reduce their risk of a life-altering event like a heart attack or stroke.”

If one thread runs through Nancy’s story, it’s the one so many women will recognize: the tendency to take care of everyone else first. “Women wear a lot of hats, and most of them involve caring for other people,” she says. “We don’t always stop to care for ourselves.”

That’s the habit she’s determined to break—in herself, and in the women who’ve heard important health messages from her for years. Her message today isn’t fear; it’s agency. “I want women to proactively understand their cardiovascular risk before something forces them to,” she says. “Ask the question: What’s my risk, and what can I do about it?”

Nancy’s ask is simple: Talk to your healthcare provider about your LDL-C and your personal cardiovascular risk factors. Get your LDL-C tested, know your doctor-recommended LDL-C goal and—if needed—make a plan with your doctor to help you reach it.

“This is the health story I never expected to tell,” Nancy says. “But if telling it means one more woman picks up the phone and calls her doctor, then it’s the most important one I’ve ever shared.”

What are the possible side effects of Repatha®?

Repatha® can cause serious side effects including serious allergic reactions. Stop taking Repatha® and call your healthcare provider or seek emergency help right away if you have any of these symptoms: trouble breathing or swallowing, raised bumps (hives), rash or itching, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat or arms.

The most common side effects of Repatha® include: runny nose, sore throat, symptoms of the common cold, flu or flu-like symptoms, back pain, high blood sugar levels (diabetes) and redness, pain, or bruising at the injection site.

Tell your healthcare provider if you have any side effects that bother you or that do not go away.

These are not all the possible side effects of Repatha®. Ask your healthcare provider or pharmacist for more information. Call your healthcare provider for medical advice about side effects.
